fullText:
A former Cornell University student filed a lawsuit this month alleging she was drugged and gang raped inside a fraternity house in 2024, and the fresh scrutiny has prompted prosecutors to reopen the investigation.

The 101-page lawsuit details disturbing allegations about what the woman, identified as Jane Doe, says unfolded inside Chi Phi’s frat house the night of October 19, 2024, and how the university and local prosecutors in Ithaca, New York, handled the case. Doe is accusing seven members of the frat of participating in the assault while she was unable to consent.

The Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office said Monday it reopened the case to seek a grand jury review after being “asked by the community to revisit the decision whether to pursue criminal charges against the seven fraternity members.”

County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said no criminal charges were initially filed because Doe had not provided police in 2024 with the same key allegations outlined in the new lawsuit.

Doe’s attorney says the information was promptly given to Cornell authorities, and the report was “not materially different from what is contained in the (2026) complaint.”

The legal dispute, lack of criminal charges and university’s response has prompted fierce backlash and revived concerns about how schools respond to allegations of campus sexual assault.

The complaint names more than a dozen defendants, including the seven fraternity members from 2024, Cornell University, and the Chi Phi fraternity. Allegations include negligence, breach of contract, sexual assault and battery, and violations of New York’s Human Rights Law.

CNN has sought comment from the Cornell University Police Department, the Chi Phi fraternity and others named in the lawsuit.

The complaint says Doe was 20 years old and had been drinking at her sorority house and a bar before she arrived at the Chi Phi house to visit a friend, who was one of the fraternity members, on the night of October 19, 2024.

According to the suit, Doe had already consumed about 10 standard drinks within the past three hours when she arrived at the fraternity house.

The complaint alleges the friend and another fraternity member gave her more alcohol and pressured her into snorting a substance they described as ketamine, and that she was then sexually assaulted while “incapable of consent.” A third fraternity member eventually entered the room and also sexually assaulted her, the complaint alleges.

At roughly 1:42 a.m., one of the men allegedly sent a message to the fraternity’s Snapchat group chat a message – titled “Chi Phi Actives” – stating there was “free p*ssy” upstairs.

A photo of a portion of the chat is included in the filing. Multiple fraternity members then entered the room, where one of the newcomers kissed her without her consent, and one of the first three men commanded her to take more ketamine and groped her, according to the complaint.

The seven defendants in the complaint poured ketamine onto her body and snorted it, the complaint says.

Eventually, five defendants left the room, and the remaining two men led her to a different room, where those two instructed her to take more ketamine and sexually assaulted her until about 5:45 a.m., the complaint says.

An attorney for one of the accused fraternity brothers denied any wrongdoing by his client.

“Even the district attorney’s office, led by a chief prosecutor with the duty to pursue justice and uphold the rule of law without bias or favor, filed no charges against (him) because what she alleged did not happen,” attorney Jeremy Saland said in a statement to CNN. He said his client “never sexually assaulted or even touched the plaintiff in any way.”

An attorney for a different student gave ABC News a statement acknowledging that student participated in the Snapchat conversation mentioned in the complaint but denying that he engaged in sexual activity.

“I did not participate in any sexual activity or drug use. I was not found responsible by Cornell for any of the accusations involving sexual activity and drug use for which others received serious consequences,” the student said through his attorney. “I thoughtlessly engaged in Snapchat and briefly stopped in the room where misconduct happened but not when it happened.”

CNN is working to determine if the other fraternity brothers have representation.

The district attorney said the initial report Jane Doe made to university police differs significantly from the allegations in the lawsuit.

Nothing in Doe’s original statement indicated she was drugged without consent or had sex against her will, Van Houten said. According to the accuser’s statement, “each time Jane Doe asked to stop the sexual conduct, the sexual conduct stopped.”

Van Houten’s office has not released the full police report. CNN has asked Doe’s attorney for a response to Van Houten’s statement and for a copy of her complete 2024 police statement.

During a contentious interview Monday, CNN’s Jake Tapper pressed Van Houten on why there wasn’t a more expansive investigation from law enforcement or the DA’s office after the initial report was made in 2024.

“We can’t change what happened in the past as much as the community is outraged,” Van Houten said. “My job under the New York State Constitution is to apply the penal law of New York state. We are constrained by that law. Whether you agree with it, whether you think someone’s conduct is morally repugnant or vulgar or disgusting. I’m still constrained by the law.”

Van Houten acknowledged that the text message screen shots between the men “were completely vulgar and disgusting, but they had nothing to do with her consent.”

Tapper asked when Van Houten got copies of the text messages, included in the complaint, that the fraternity brothers sent each other.

Van Houten said that his team did not see the text messages evidence initially.

“They were not part of our initial analysis, but I understand that Cornell had them, and they sent them to our team,” he said.

Earlier, Doe’s attorney, Thomas P. Giuffra said in a statement he believes the initial investigation was inadequate.

“It is challenging for me to understand how a thorough criminal investigation could have been conducted when she never spoke with anyone other than the officer who took her original complaint,” Giuffra said.

“Other than her initial contact with Cornell police, she was not contacted by investigators from the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office or any investigators trained in interviewing rape survivors,” Giuffra said.

“If the district attorney’s office is now considering prosecution, I believe that it is a step in the right direction, albeit a late one.”

The Ithaca Police Department said Monday that it was “disturbed” to hear about the 2024 allegations. The department noted it learned about the alleged incident only recently through the media and said the incident was not reported to the agency.

Doe reported the incident to Cornell University police on November 8, 2024, the complaint says.

Doe’s attorney said Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students while the others received lesser punishment, including suspensions, workshops or written assignments.

Cornell countered that claim Monday, saying there was a range of sanctions for the accused students, including suspensions and expulsions. But “none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement,” the university said.

In a September 21 statement, Cornell declined to confirm the individual disciplinary outcomes, citing federal student privacy law. The school said violations of university policy “could lead to sanctions up to and including suspension or expulsion,” adding, “We will respond in detail through the legal process.”

The sanctions came after it conducted a formal Title IX investigation, separate from the criminal proceeding, and a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days, the school said.

The school also said it had closed the chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity, and that the chapter remains barred from campus.

The lawsuit faults Cornell for failing to properly discipline after the assault, “all the while sheltering them from speaking to law enforcement, and silencing victims.”

Cornell’s “conduct was so outrageous, shocking, despicable, and contemptible that it exceeds the reasonable bounds of decency as measured by what the average member of the community would tolerate and demonstrates an utter disregard for the consequences that would follow,” the lawsuit says.

The complaint is seeking a jury trial to determine monetary damages.

Cornell said Monday it “supports the decision of the Tompkins County District Attorney (DA) to provide an opportunity for the victim’s story … to be heard by a criminal grand jury.”

“Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” Cornell said in a release. “A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault.”

The lawsuit — along with a lack of criminal charges and accusations of inadequate discipline — has drawn a wave of outrage.

Cornell student Hayden Watkins, executive vice president of the Student Assembly, said many students are talking about the allegations and the feeling on campus is “pretty grim.”

“I think a lot of people are upset about it knowing that it happened on campus, and truthfully I think a lot of people feel not enough was done,” Watkins said.

Ithaca Mayor Robert G. Cantelmo on Monday called for a pause on Cornell University’s Greek life and student group gatherings.

The mayor said on Instagram that the moratorium would be in place “until such time that the University conducts an accounting of its protocols to prevent and prosecute crimes of sexual violence and publicly releases new standards and practices to keep our community safe.”

A Cornell spokesperson said the university “shares the mayor’s interest in student well-being and safety,” and that the university “will work with him to address his concerns.”

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called the allegations “horrifying,” and said she supported the district attorney’s decision to reopen the criminal investigation.

“No student should ever be left wondering whether the institutions meant to protect them will listen and act,” she said in a release.

She also called for outside counsel to conduct an independent review of the university’s response, saying there are “serious questions about Cornell’s campus culture and its systems for prevention, reporting, and response.”

US Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a Democrat from New York City, condemned what she described as a “culture of rape” at elite universities and institutions during a Sunday town hall in Ithaca.

“Those men posted in a group chat,” Ocasio-Cortez said, referencing allegations in the lawsuit. “That means it was normal to them, that means it was acceptable to them. This is a culture, this is norms, these are practices, and what we must do is understand that we cannot protect those spaces anymore.”

Actor Florence Pugh also posted an impassioned statement on Instagram Sunday, writing, “I’m no longer tired – I’m enraged by schools protecting boys, in fear of their futures being wrecked.”

“What about the life that those girls then have to endure, with the knowledge that his reputation is more precious than her truth?” she added.

Pugh also addressed Doe directly, calling her “so unbelievably powerful” and “so strong willed.”

“Know that women everywhere are here to hold you and help you on your healing journey,” she wrote.

Help is available: For help in the US, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673 or chat 24/7 on online.rainn.org.

CNN’s Jeff Winter and Cindy Von Quednow contributed to this report.

title: Reports surface that Netanyahu ignored Oct. 7 attack warnings to dominate Israeli election
description:
JERUSALEM - A slew of reports that Arab officials warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about a serious threat emerging from Gaza days before the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas have put the longtime Israeli leader on the defensive less than 30 days before a pivotal election. 
Ever since the attack, the most deadly in Israel’s history, Netanyahu has argued that Israeli security chiefs collectively failed to foresee the surprise attack by Hamas - but that he led the fightback, scoring redemptive battlefield victories in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Iran.
Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. 
But that narrative is fraying as reports of the advance warnings, including one delivered by United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, train a spotlight on Netanyahu’s handling of the attack and his refusal to allow an independent commission to investigate it.
fullText:
JERUSALEM - A slew of reports that Arab officials warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about a serious threat emerging from Gaza days before the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas have put the longtime Israeli leader on the defensive less than 30 days before a pivotal election.

Ever since the attack, the most deadly in Israel's history, Netanyahu has argued that Israeli security chiefs collectively failed to foresee the surprise attack by Hamas - but that he led the fightback, scoring redemptive battlefield victories in Gaza, Lebanon, Syria and Iran.

But that narrative is fraying as reports of the advance warnings, including one delivered by United Arab Emirates President Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, train a spotlight on Netanyahu's handling of the attack and his refusal to allow an independent commission to investigate it.

Netanyahu and his office have denied the reports, and his political party and supporters have accused "left-wing" Israeli officials, as well as journalists and overseas interests, of conspiring to oust him from office through a coordinated smear campaign ahead of the Oct. 27 election.

The disclosures began to trickle out in early September, when the Israeli newspaper Haaretz published an excerpt from "Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment," a book by two Israeli journalists that details an encrypted call reportedly made by the Emirati president, who is known as MBZ, less than two weeks before Oct. 7, 2023, to warn Netanyahu that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was planning a major operation that could destabilize the Middle East. Netanyahu did not pass on the warnings to his security aides, according to the book authors, Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval.

"We have excellent proof and many more scoops in the book," Eldar said. "It's rock solid." The UAE Foreign Ministry did not deny the Haaretz excerpt, saying, "When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities."

In recent days, the debate in Israel has reached a fever pitch after the Atlantic and the Wall Street Journal published reports that then-Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel also warned Netanyahu about Gaza in the days before Oct. 7.

On Sunday, Netanyahu flew to Abu Dhabi and requested that MBZ explicitly deny that a warning call about Oct. 7 took place in late 2023, said a person with knowledge of the meeting who, like others quoted in this article, spoke on the condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter.

Netanyahu's office denied that Netanyahu made such a request, calling it "fake news." When asked about the Sunday meeting, the UAE Foreign Ministry referred The Washington Post to a report by the official Emirates News Agency released late Monday saying the two leaders had discussed "bilateral relations and ways to strengthen ties." The ministry declined further comment.

Several senior Israeli officials, including the former army chief of staff and head of military intelligence, have resigned, saying they failed to protect the country.

Netanyahu, by contrast, has deflected responsibility and repeatedly accused his security chiefs of missing the threat from Gaza and even "deliberately" letting him sleep for four hours after Hamas began its assault on southern Israel at 6:30 a.m. on Oct. 7.

On Monday, Ronen Bar, the former director of Shin Bet, Israel's domestic intelligence agency, sued Netanyahu for defamation, accusing the prime minister of "trying to deflect fire from himself by hurling accusations at the person who warned him in real time."

It's not immediately clear how the allegations will affect polls, which have held relatively steady in recent weeks and show former military chief Gadi Eisenkot's party narrowly leading Netanyahu's Likud. The reports, however, have dominated headlines and prime-time talk shows.

Several security branches, including the Israel Defense Forces and Shin Bet, have conducted internal probes into their failures to anticipate the Oct. 7 attack, but Netanyahu's government has refused to authorize one for itself.

Many of Netanyahu's campaign rivals, including Eisenkot, have pledged to immediately establish an independent commission of inquiry if elected.

Jonathan Rynhold, a political scientist at Bar-Ilan University, said Netanyahu may be hobbled by the claims about the warnings, but his loyal base and Israel's predominantly right-leaning voters may not jump ship for the centrist bloc led by Eisenkot without a "clear smoking gun."

"Oct. 7 has been on everybody's mind every day for three years, so it is relevant, but these claims have been bubbling for a long time in different forms," Rynhold said. "Imagine there's a video of all the Egyptians and the Emiratis and you can actually see him getting the warning and it was repeated 50 times on social media, then it becomes unavoidable. But obviously that's not what's going to happen."

Sufian Abu Zaida, a former Palestinian official who was the source of the warning that eventually reached the UAE, told The Post that he met Sinwar, the Hamas leader, in his Gaza City office in September 2023, and Sinwar dictated an offer to Israeli negotiators: he would release two Israeli soldiers and two civilians held in Gaza in exchange for Israel freeing Palestinian prisoners and lifting its heavy trade and movement restrictions imposed on the strip since 2007. Otherwise, Sinwar warned, there would be an "earthquake."

"The exact content of the message was: "We will put cards on the table, there will be an earthquake regarding the negotiations and we will empty the [Israeli] prisons [of Palestinians]," Abu Zaida recalled in an interview this week, adding that Sinwar told him to "make sure" the message reached the Israelis.

Abu Zaida said he passed the message to Shin Bet officials and also relayed it to an adviser to MBZ in Abu Dhabi - the Palestinian politician Mohammad Dahlan, who then informed the UAE president. Abu Zaida said he also passed the message to Samir al-Mashharawi, a Palestinian political leader and Dahlan associate based in Egypt.

The three Palestinian intermediaries "didn't know that Sinwar was ready to go ahead with his threats, or how and when," Abu Zaida said. "I was thinking that it might be about the West Bank: kidnapping a soldier from here or there for later negotiations with Israel for a prisoner exchange."

Several months after Oct. 7, in early 2024, MBZ recounted to then-CIA Director William J. Burns that he had warned Netanyahu about the possibility of violence erupting but did not include specific details that anticipated the Oct. 7 plot, a person familiar with the matter said.

The Emirates' refusal to disavow the reports of advance warnings is particularly striking because it is the Arab country that has stood closest to Netanyahu over the past three years even as his international standing plummeted.

Since signing the Abraham Accords that normalized diplomatic relations with Israel in 2020, the UAE has often been more measured in its criticism of Israel's conduct in Gaza and the West Bank than some other Arab countries that have accused Israel of genocide and ethnic cleansing.

At other times, the UAE has taken a relatively tougher stance toward Israel's foes, such as Iran, and it has supported the U.S.-Israeli-led war.

Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute in Washington, noted that Emirati officials have declined to hand Netanyahu a political favor by explicitly denying the reports of the warnings.

"The reality is that Netanyahu is a liability for the UAE right now," Vatanka said. "They are sensitive to their image in the Islamic world and don't want to be seen as too close with Netanyahu."

But, he added, the UAE is "not going to walk away from its relationship" with the state of Israel itself.

Back home, Netanyahu's supporters kicked into damage-control mode.

"As the elections approach, we are seeing a flood of false reports by mobilized left-wing journalists, aimed at toppling the right and installing a Left-Muslim Brotherhood government that will surrender on every front," the Likud Party said in a statement.

Amit Segal, a political commentator who is seen as close to Netanyahu, said there were "Arab nations" behind the "slanderous fabrications" and warned that if the Israeli right lost the elections, a Palestinian state would emerge.

"This is the election question: It is either the Right or Palestine," Segal posted on social media.

Eldar, the Israeli author, said Likud lawyers have threatened to sue him for defamation and accused him of seeking to influence the election. He said he first obtained information about the call almost two years ago and it took the publisher until this month to release the book.

"I would have preferred to publish it a year ago, but it took time," Eldar said.

One Israeli political consultant, who is not affiliated with a campaign in this election cycle and who spoke on the condition of anonymity to preserve client relationships, said Netanyahu's campaign might find ways to benefit from the fallout of the new claims.

The controversy could draw attention away from the intense criticism Netanyahu has faced over his government's policy of allowing ultra-Orthodox Jews to forgo mandatory military service, and Netanyahu could instead focus attention on Oct. 7 and the danger posed by Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 21 percent of the Israeli population, the consultant said.

Polls show that to form a majority government, Eisenkot may need to join hands with the so-called Arab parties, which Netanyahu's campaign has frequently portrayed as security risks in campaign ads with racist undertones.

The furor over the pre-Oct. 7 warnings "seems negative, but it's also changed the narrative" in Israel, the consultant said. "Netanyahu can push aside the ultra-Orthodox issue and bring to the table the conversation about the fact that Gadi Eisenkot doesn't have a majority without the voice or fingers of the Arab parties."

Lior Soroka contributed to this report.

title: Boreham Wood sign Barnet defender Wright
description: Boreham Wood sign Barnet defender Will Wright on a three-year deal, after less than three months at the League Two side.
fullText:
Boreham Wood have signed defender Will Wright from League Two side Barnet on a three-year deal.

Wright, 29, only joined the Bees in July but made just one start and five substitute appearances.

He has played 80 times in League Two for Swindon Town, Crawley Town and Gillingham, and 135 times in the National League with Dagenham & Redbridge.

Wright now returns to the fifth tier after Boreham Wood agreed an undisclosed fee with Barnet for the centre-back.

title: Lindsay Clancy's defense shifts strategy in bid to avert retrial
description:
Lindsay Clancy's lawyers argued on Tuesday that prosecutors had not proven the Massachusetts woman killed her three children in 2023, in a shift from their previous defense that she was not criminally responsible because of mental illness.
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington made that argument during the ‌first hearing in Clancy's case since a judge in Plymouth, Massachusetts, declared a mistrial on September 4 because a single juror prevented the 12-member jury from unanimously ‌deciding whether to convict Clancy or find her not guilty by reason of insanity.
No one at that trial disputed that Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in ​the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.
But Reddington told Judge William Sullivan that prosecutors failed to present any evidence at the trial proving she had in fact killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan, saying police conducted a "horrific, ridiculous investigation" that failed to collect evidence showing she killed them.
fullText:
Sept 29 (Reuters) - Lindsay Clancy's lawyers argued on Tuesday that prosecutors had not proven the Massachusetts woman killed her three children in 2023, in a shift from their previous defense that she was not criminally responsible because of mental illness.

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington made that argument during the ‌first hearing in Clancy's case since a judge in Plymouth, Massachusetts, declared a mistrial on September 4 because a single juror prevented the 12-member jury from unanimously ‌deciding whether to convict Clancy or find her not guilty by reason of insanity.

No one at that trial disputed that Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands on January 24, 2023, in the basement of their home in ​the Boston suburb of Duxbury. She then cut herself with a knife and jumped from a second-story window in an attempt to end her own life, leaving her paralyzed.

But Reddington told Judge William Sullivan that prosecutors failed to present any evidence at the trial proving she had in fact killed Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and 8-month-old Callan, saying police conducted a "horrific, ridiculous investigation" that failed to collect evidence showing she killed them.

"This entire case is based on speculation," Reddington said. "Where is the admission?"

Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham called the argument "laughable" and said it was being raised for the first time at ‌the hearing. During the weeks-long trial, Reddington had instead argued that ⁠Clancy was in the throes of postpartum psychosis and did not know what she was doing was wrong.

Reddington also maintained that argument during the hearing, telling Sullivan that every doctor who testified at the trial indicated Clancy was suffering from a serious mental disease or defect at the time.

"The ⁠evidence shows clearly and unequivocally that she was in a state of psychosis," he said.

Buckingham said prosecutors had not disputed that Clancy had mental health issues. But she said the evidence showed that Clancy knew what she was doing and had decided to kill the children after deciding to take her own life.

"She had succumbed to the idea that she didn't want to be here anymore, that she was going to ​commit ​suicide, and that she was going to take those kids with her because no one could care for ​them like she could," Buckingham said.

Sullivan did not immediately rule on the ‌defense's request to declare Clancy not guilty. But he stressed that he did not want the case to linger and told Clancy's attorneys and prosecutors under Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz to be ready to discuss a date for a retrial when they reconvene for another hearing on November 2.

"I think it's important that this case move forward if it has to move forward," Sullivan said.

QUESTIONS REMAIN OVER HOLDOUT JUROR

If convicted on first-degree murder charges, Clancy would face a sentence of life in prison.

Several jurors in televised interviews after the initial trial said that but for the one holdout juror, they had been prepared to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, known in Massachusetts as lack of criminal responsibility.

If found not guilty on those grounds, she ‌would be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for evaluation. Her commitment would then be subject to regular ​review by the court.

Prosecutors have several options before them, including trying to reach a plea deal or retrying ​Clancy on lesser second-degree murder charges, which would give her the option to waive a ​jury trial and proceed before a judge.

Clancy's lawyers have filed a series of motions seeking to head off the possibility of a retrial and ‌have also asked the judge to conduct a "limited inquiry" concerning the holdout juror.

Sullivan ​said he would take up that issue and ​other motions at the November 2 hearing, as well as a request by prosecutors for a gag order to prevent the "carnival atmosphere" that enveloped her first televised trial and protect the potential jury pool, which they said had been "inevitably tainted."

Prosecutors said the jury pool was polluted as a result of a series of televised interviews in which Reddington ​characterized Clancy as a "wonderful" person, asked President Donald Trump to pardon ‌her, and, "most disturbingly," spoke about the holdout juror "in ways that ensured that juror would be publicly identified."

In a video statement to Fox News' Sean Hannity that aired ​late on Monday, the holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, acknowledged that since the mistrial the focus of attention had shifted to him instead of "on the three angels."

(Reporting ​by Nate Raymond in Boston; Editing by Alexia Garamfalvi, Cynthia Osterman, Bill Berkrot and Deepa Babington)

title: Man City found guilty of all charges
description: The Premier League has confirmed that Manchester City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18.  In a statement on its website, the Premier League said an independent commission has found City entered into "sham" contracts and agreements to "inflate the club's revenue and reduce its costs".  City were found to have "misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances", with the commission stating the club were "significantly" in breach of both Premier League and Uefa rules.
fullText:
The Premier League has confirmed that Manchester City have been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18.

In a statement on its website, the Premier League said an independent commission has found City entered into "sham" contracts and agreements to "inflate the club's revenue and reduce its costs".

City were found to have "misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances", with the commission stating the club were "significantly" in breach of both Premier League and Uefa rules.

City have until Friday to appeal.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said: "The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade.

"It also vindicates the Premier League's decision to pursue this case against Manchester City. While the process to date has been both long and difficult, the League has remained determined that the facts be established independently.

"It is a key responsibility of the Premier League to ensure that the Rules, approved by the clubs themselves, are upheld to protect the integrity of the competition. It is paramount that the League remains competitive and fair for all clubs and for the fans. We take that role extremely seriously.

"This disciplinary case, and this decision, are the most significant in Premier League history. There are elements of the case that remain to be decided, including, importantly, what sanction must follow for these breaches. Now we have the Commission's decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the League, our clubs and fans."

title: GOP senator's conspiracy theory about Jack Smith unravels during hearing
description: A Republican senator's attempt to throw evidence at a long-running conspiracy theory against Jack Smith blew up in his face during a heated congressional hearing Tuesday.
fullText:
A Republican senator's attempt to throw evidence at a long-running conspiracy theory against Jack Smith blew up in his face during a heated congressional hearing Tuesday.

A phenomenal moment in the Senate.

Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., claims he has evidence Jack Smith went to a HAWKS game in Atlanta.

Smith denies it.

Schmitt declares he has busted Jack Smith for perjury.

Smith, vexed, says he went to HAWKEYES game in Maryland.

Watch the whole thing: pic.twitter.com/J07o5Uwfxi

— Sahil Kapur (@sahilkapur) September 29, 2026

Senator Eric Schmitt, who accused the former special counsel of perjury and labeled him a "total dirtbag," invoked a conspiracy theory that Smith's team conspired with state prosecutors in Georgia — and claimed that he had evidence that Smith was attending an NBA game in Atlanta at the time.

In the middle of Tuesday's Senate Judiciary Committee, Schmitt held up a poster board containing what he claimed were text messages from Smith's staff stating that the special counsel was attending an Atlanta Hawks NBA game — and suggested that he colluded with Fulton County District Attorney Fani Willis to prosecute the president and his allies.

Smith was attending a basketball game that day. But it was the Iowa Hawkeyes, not the Hawks. And it was in Maryland.

Schmitt, who was corrected by Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar, shouted out across the panel as the pair argued over his claims.

"Perhaps you should have looked at it more carefully," Klobuchar told him.

"Whose questioning is this, by the way?" Schmitt yelled out. "Are we just having an open session here? Well, I'm glad you're trying to rehabilitate the witness."

"I think that people should have their facts straight before they accuse someone of being a dirtbag," Klobuchar said. "You have your teams wrong, sir."

The former special counsel faced another round of attacks from Republican members of the committee who have characterized him as a leading figure in what Trump has called the "weaponization" of the Department of Justice against his allies.

"You make me want to throw up in my mouth," Louisiana Senator John Kennedy told him.

"You make what President Nixon did at Watergate look like a Sunday picnic," added Senator Mike Lee.

Smith has repeatedly testified that he never traveled to Atlanta while serving as special counsel overseeing indictments against Trump, who faced criminal charges over his attempts to overturn the results of the 2020 election and failure to stop a mob of his supporters from storming the Capitol on January 6, 2021.

The president also faced 40 separate charges stemming from allegations that he withheld hundreds of documents at his Mar-a-Lago compound after leaving office, and then obstructed federal law enforcement efforts to retrieve them.

After Trump won the 2024 election, Smith filed motions to dismiss both cases altogether, a decision that appeared inevitable; the special counsel's office determined he could not prosecute a sitting president. Smith then completed his reports on the investigations, submitted them to the Office of Attorney General and resigned.

Willis, meanwhile, failed to keep herself on the Georgia case following a lengthy court battle after she admitted to hiring a former romantic partner as a special prosecutor.

Schmitt, whose staff briefly held up a poster board of text messages that was not shown to other members, suggested Smith had traveled to Atlanta after Willis "came clean."

He then suggested Smith was lying to the panel.

"You may think you're a hero in this story. But let me tell you something, you've done so much damage," he told Smith. "You will go down as a total dirtbag."

The Hawks played the Golden State Warriors inside Atlanta's State Farm Arena on February 3, 2024.

The Iowa Hawkeyes women's basketball team played the Maryland Tarrapins that same day — but in College Park, Maryland.

"I recall going to a University of Maryland basketball game where Caitlin Clark was playing right around that time, and the Marshals Service was there with me, you could check," Smith testified.

"For a U.S. senator to have false information and imply, based on a confusion about the name of a team, that you were in another city and somehow involved that day in what was happening in Georgia and then call you a 'dirtbag' is something that deserves an apology," Klobuchar said.

A crusade from Trump's Republican allies in Congress to prosecute Smith kicked off last year, when Senate Republicans falsely accused the former special counsel and FBI investigators of "tapping" their phones.

Instead, Smith's team sought a "preliminary toll analysis" of phone records, which only include what numbers were called and when and for how long. They do not include the contents of messages or conversations, which would require a court-approved wiretap.

Senator Dick Durbin, the committee's top Democrat, called attacks against him "petty, personal and political."

"They are nothing but a smokescreen but to distract from the president's own, clear unlawful conduct," Durbin said in his opening remarks.

Smith has defended the investigations, stating that prosecutors uncovered evidence that the president "engaged in serious crimes against our nation."

"If asked whether to prosecute a former president today based on the same facts I would do so regardless if that president was a Republican or a Democrat," Smith said in his opening statement Tuesday.

"I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the president and others," he said. "I myself have been threatened with jail by the president of the United States, but I remain confident in the rule of law."

In his first TV interview earlier this year, Smith told MS NOW's Nicole Wallace that "we are facing an attack on the rule of law that is different in kind and scope to anything I've seen in my lifetime."

When it comes to what Trump will do in midterm elections, Smith said the states should be "proactive" and be prepared to litigate "where it's appropriate and where it would make sense to, if you have a sense or reason to believe that something's going to be done to interfere with people's right to vote and participate in democracy," he said.

title: Iranian spokesman urges Americans to rally against Trump's policies in address
description: Iran's Revolutionary Guard urged Americans in a message ahead of U.S. midterm elections to take to the streets and rally against Donald Trump, claiming the U.S. president's war in the Middle East has failed.
fullText:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard urged Americans in a message ahead of U.S. midterm elections to take to the streets and rally against Donald Trump, claiming the U.S. president's war in the Middle East has failed.

Meanwhile, in the occupied West Bank, settlers rioted, throwing rocks, blocking roads and setting Palestinian property on fire to prevent a Palestinian man escorted by the Israeli military from returning to his home in the village of Jalud.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Tuesday. Full coverage is available here.

Gen. Hossein Mohebbi, spokesman for the Revolutionary Guard, held a news conference in Tehran, Iran's capital, on Tuesday and read from what he said was a "letter to the American people."

Reading from the prepared text, he said that the only way for the war to end is for Washington to admit defeat and leave. The message was apparently meant for the U.S. public just weeks ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections for the U.S. Senate and Congress — a vote in which Trump's Republican Party faces fierce headwinds as it looks to maintain control of Congress.

Later, in remarks to The Associated Press, Mohebbi urged Americans to take to the streets and protest Trump's policies to denounce what he called the U.S. government's war-mongering policies.

Mohebbi also said Americans should "revise their decision" about their leaders.

He accused the United States of using Iran's nuclear program as a ruse to "plunder Iran's wealth" and to turn the country "back into a colony." The U.S. military action and economic sanctions would not get Tehran to submit.

Meanwhile, Iran's currency fell to a new record low Tuesday, with traders in Tehran exchanging more than 2.5 million rials to the U.S. dollar, a sign of how the conflict has further eroded Iran's economy.

The decline came after the rial hit its previous record low of 2.2 million to the dollar on Sept. 2. The currency has repeatedly reached new lows since the war began in February.

Over a hundred Israeli settlers scuffled with Israeli soldiers who were trying to escort a Palestinian man to his home in the West Bank village of Jalud.

The homeowner, Mahmoud Tubasi, told the AP that the soldiers initially brought him to his home but that rioting settlers forced him to leave with his family in a military vehicle. He said he still can't access the house, which settlers have besieged for two months.

Israel's military acknowledged that the overnight mission to return the family "was not completed" and that three officers were injured by settlers who threw rocks, blocked roads and set Palestinian property on fire.

Israeli police said they arrested three settlers suspected of participating in the riot, which was condemned by Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Foreign Minister Gidon Saar and President Isaac Herzog.

The Israeli military has struggled to quell the latest wave of settler violence. Rights groups have accused the military of colluding with the settlers.

An Israeli strike on an apartment west of Gaza City killed two people, including a Hamas commander who the Israeli military said was involved in plotting attacks and recruiting new members for the militant group.

Al-Shifa Hospital officials said Tuesday the strike also wounded five others.

Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz said the overnight strike targeted Izz al-Din Bik, a commander in the Hamas militant group's northern Gaza brigade.

Hamas confirmed the death of al-Bik, claiming in a statement he was one of the main overseers of the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks on southern Israel, which killed over 1,200 and prompted the war in Gaza.

More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since a ceasefire took effect nearly a year ago, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, while over 74,000 Palestinians have been killed since the war began. The ministry maintains detailed records that are generally seen as reliable. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants, but says women and children make up around half of the fatalities.

A mass funeral was held Tuesday in Gaza's Nuseirat refugee camp for nearly 50 people killed during the war.

The remains, wrapped in white bags and draped with Palestinian flags, were recovered last week from the rubble of buildings destroyed almost three years ago.

Mass funerals have become more common in Gaza, where Israel has not allowed the heavy machinery needed to clear the rubble of destroyed buildings and recover the dead.

Earlier this month, the United Nations estimated that more than 8,000 bodies remain buried under the debris.

For some, partial remains were all they had to bury.

Areej Farajallah said two of her husband's bones were found last week. She is also mourning her child, who was among those buried Tuesday.

Abdel-Nasser al-Tawil said his home was hit Oct. 15, 2023, in the early days of the war. He said he recovered 13 bodies Tuesday with the help of the Red Cross and Palestinian Civil Defense workers ahead of the funeral.

This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

title: GOP senators push back on Trump's taxpayer-funded ads
description:
President Trump's new government-funded ads pledging to “cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists” are getting strong pushback from Senate Republicans who are warning the president not to use taxpayer money to promote himself in such a brazenly political way.
While Republicans generally approve of Trump’s political message, they say using taxpayer dollars to fund a series of ads that closely resemble Trump’s past campaign advertising right before the midterm elections is inappropriate.
“It’s a great message, I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters Monday.
fullText:
President Trump’s new government-funded ads pledging to “cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists” are getting strong pushback from Senate Republicans who are warning the president not to use taxpayer money to promote himself in such a brazenly political way.

While Republicans generally approve of Trump’s political message, they say using taxpayer dollars to fund a series of ads that closely resemble Trump’s past campaign advertising right before the midterm elections is inappropriate.

“It’s a great message, I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told reporters Monday.

The White House, however, argues the ads — which ran over the weekend during “Fox News Sunday” and several college and NFL football games — are “very clearly not campaign ads” and instead “a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending.”

Republican senators are not buying that argument, and warn that it creates an improper appearance to be using taxpayer money to pay for television ads that could easily be confused with regular campaign ads, even though Trump himself is not on the ballot.

“It would not have been something that I would have done,” said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.). “I know that the White House is not covered by the same guidance that we are, but it’s not something I would have done.”

“I just don’t think it’s right to be using taxpayer money in that way, particularly if it’s tied to political campaigns,” he added. “I think they need to rethink that strategy.”

Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said using taxpayer money to fund a television ad that’s nearly identical to the ad that Trump posted to social media during his presidential campaign and echoes the rhetoric he has used at election-year rallies crosses a red line.

“We all know you’re not supposed to use taxpayer money for that purpose,” the Republican senator noted.

Cornyn said he doesn’t know exactly where the money to produce and air the ads is coming from but added “if it comes from taxpayers, it shouldn’t.”

The latest advertisement, which ran on television over the weekend, is part of a series of ads that come with the disclaimer: “Paid by the U.S. Government.”

It is nearly identical to an online ad that Trump posted to his Truth Social account in January 2024, when he was preparing to launch his presidential campaign. In that online ad, he urged supporters to text “TRUMP to 88022” to support his campaign.

The ad features Trump walking down hallway while an audio clip plays of a speech he delivered at an unidentified event pledging: “This is the final battle. With you at my side, we will demolish the deep state, we will expel the warmongers from our government. We will drive out the globalists, we will cast out the communists, Marxists and fascists.”

“We will liberate America from these villains once and for all,” Trump is heard declaring as an unseen audience cheers in the background.

The latest iteration of the ad, however, ends with a disclaimer informing viewers that it was “paid for by the U.S. government.”

The White House aired its first ad of the new series last week — a 30-second television spot that featured a montage of pictures of the president, interspersed with Trump’s declaration that “together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America” and that “America will never be a communist country.”

The ad was paired with the song “Love Me” by JMSN and ended with a voiceover of UFC President Dana White extolling Trump as the “toughest, most resilient person I have ever met.”

The White House responded to criticisms in a statement.

“The attacks on President Donald J. Trump’s public service announcements are highly dishonest. The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action,” the White House argued.

The White House noted that the George W. Bush administration ran a national television campaign explaining the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act to seniors — one of former President Bush’s signature legislative accomplishments — in March 2004, when Bush was up for reelection later that year.

The White House also pointed out that the Obama administration used national advertising to promote subsidies under the Affordable Care Act (ACA) in 2015 and the start of open enrollment under the ACA in 2016.

Republican Sen. John Curtis (Utah) said constituents “are worried about affordability and they don’t want to be worried about how their taxpayer dollars are being spent.”

“If it were me as a senator, it would be a problem,” he said of using taxpayer money to fund ads that appear to be political in nature.

“I don’t know their rules as well as I know mine, but I know mine would prohibit that,” he added.

A Senate GOP aide who requested anonymity to discuss the matter said the new Trump promotional ads paid for by the federal government appear “very similar” in nature to the promotional ads that then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem ran last year to tout her leadership of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Trump fired Noem after she was grilled about the expenditure of public funds for the promotional ad blitz, which was estimated to cost more than $220 million.

Republican Sen. John Kennedy (La.), a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee who challenged Noem over DHS’s advertising campaign in March, said he disagreed with the Trump administration’s use of public funds for the new series of ads.

“I don’t think any public official, including President Trump … should spend public money on private ads for themselves,” Kennedy said Sunday on CBS News’s “Face the Nation.”

“The White House sees it differently,” he added.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) called on the Justice Department to investigate whether the use of taxpayer money to pay for ads promoting rhetoric similar to what Trump has used at political events violates the law.

“There should be a full investigation because on its face it appears to be a violation of federal law,” she said.

“The Department of Justice, the folks that enforce federal law, should be the ones” to lead the investigation, she said.

“This is the problem when the attorney general says his duty of loyalty is not to the people of the United States but instead is to Donald Trump personally,” she added, referring to Attorney General Todd Blanche.

Richard Painter, a White House ethics lawyer who served under Bush, wrote on social platform X that the use of taxpayer money to promote the president’s political message shortly before the midterm election “could be an impeachable offense.”

“@POTUS has no right to use taxpayer money for campaign ads. Congress has expressly prohibited government sponsored political propaganda, which is dangerous for democracy,” he warned.

title: 10 Hacks Every Canva User Should Know
description: Level up your design capabilities with these hidden hacks.
fullText:
Canva is one of the most popular design tools for creating everything from flyers and business cards to interactive presentations. It's pretty user-friendly even for those who don't have any design experience, but if you want to level up your Canva experience, consider these tips and tricks.

If you've ever tried to manually align multiple images, text boxes, or other design elements so they're evenly spaced, only to have them off by a tiny margin with each adjustment, the "Tidy up" tool is the solution to your problem. With this feature, you can group elements, and Canva will automatically snap them into place so you don't have to shift them pixel by pixel. Select three or more elements in your design, click Position in the toolbar, and choose Tidy Up. You'll also find a bunch of other alignment and spacing options on this menu.

For designs that need to be replicated with unique information—such as matching business cards for different employees or localized marketing flyers with a consistent design—use the Bulk Create tool to generate and fill in a template instead of manually editing each individual file. Bulk Create pulls data from an Excel or CSV file (or a compatible data app, like Google Analytics) and matches it to form fields on your design. You can use Canva's AI match or drag and drop data fields manually, then preview and generate the design.

If you find an image or graphic that you like, you can filter your search to see more assets from that same artist, so all of the illustrations in your design look cohesive. This is especially useful if you are creating a manual, guide, or series of social media posts that you want to keep visually consistent. Hover over the visual element and tap the three dots, then select View more by or See more like this. You can also star the artist to easily find them again.

If you're basing your design around a photo or image, you don't have to trial-and-error your way to finding the right colors for other elements. Canva has a free custom color palette generator that analyzes uploaded images and creates four-color combinations, complete with names and hex codes. You can apply the palette to a Canva design or save it for future use. If you already have a photo in your design, select the photo, click the color swatch, and look for Photo colors on the toolbar to see the palette.

Once you settle on the style and format of text and elements in your design, use "Copy Style" to apply them across the board without needing to manually select each individual setting, such as background colors, font styles and sizes, text colors, and alignment. Select the element or text you want to copy, then click the paint roller icon in the floating toolbar and choose the element or text you want to copy the formatting into. Canva also has a "Style Match" tool that uses AI to match the visual style of existing elements.

If you have multiple team members working on the same Canva file but don't want anyone to accidentally move or resize elements while editing text, you can lock only certain elements in place while still allowing the content itself to be changed. Select the element you want to lock—such as a text box, image, or graphic—and select Lock position only. Collaborators can edit text or unlocked elements without affecting those parts that are locked.

Canva's Grids feature divides your design into compartments, such as rows or columns, which you can use to place and align images, videos, color fills, or other elements with consistent, even spacing. Grids can also be used to easily crop images or retain custom filters and effects even if images are swapped out. You can also change the spacing between grid cells to create consistent margins. Grid layouts can be found under Elements > Browse. This is especially useful for collages, vision boards, and visual storytelling.

If a URL is written out on your Canva design, viewers can copy and paste it to visit the website. If you want to add a hyperlink and ensure it remains clickable, you'll need to download your file as a PDF and share it in that format. No other file types support clickable hyperlinks (and social media platforms strip links out of PDFs as well). Go to Share > Download > PDF to save your design with clickable links.

Canva has a built-in QR code generator that allows you to drop custom codes into your design using your existing color palette. By default, these QR codes are static, meaning the link is permanently fixed, and you'd have to swap out the QR code and distribute the new design if you wanted to make changes. Dynamic codes use a redirect link that can be updated and also track scan data, such as click counts and location. If you add the Hovercode app to Canva (search "Dynamic QR Codes" under the Apps tab) and link a Hovercode account, you can have up to 10 dynamic QR codes available at once for free. After that, you can upgrade to a paid Hovercode tier.

When using Canva to present to a group, you can start a Live session to have audience members ask questions and leave comments as well as upvote feedback from other participants. Simply select Present > Present full screen or Presenter view > Present and click Canva Live > Start new session. This will generate an 8-digit code, which audience members can enter at canva.live to join the session. Audience chat messages and questions will show in the Presenter window.

title: 10 Shows Like 'Lioness' You Should Watch Next
description: These other thrillers have distinctive takes on crime and spycraft.
fullText:
For Lioness, TV superproducer Taylor Sheridan teamed up Oscar winner Zoe Saldaña for an action spy thriller—and it's not at all surprising that the show's a hit. Saldaña stars as Joe McNamara, a CIA senior case officer in charge of a program that deals almost exclusively in recruiting women as undercover operatives. Having just completed season three, the show is on track for a renewal...if the producers can lock down Saldaña and company. While we eagerly await word, enjoy these other thrillers with distinctive takes on crime and spycraft. Some with men!

Keira Knightley stars as Helen Webb in this genre-bender, wife of the Secretary of State for Defense of the UK—and also a secret spy in the employ of the Black Doves mercenary spy organization of the title. She learns from her handler (Sarah Lancashire) that her lover has been killed, thus potentially blowing her cover, but luckily, she has a hitman bestie (Ben Whislaw) to help her out. It's all deliberately pulpy, with a tongue-in-cheek self-awareness that lightens the tone. A second season is coming later in 2026. Stream Black Doves on Netflix.

With an entirely cinematic scope, this new adaptation of the Frederick Forsyth novel is buoyed by rather brilliant casting: Eddie Redmayne plays the Jackal, a cold and steely international assassin pursued by MI6 operative Bianca Pullman—she's played by Lashana Lynch, putting her experience as the new 007 in No Time to Die to good use. I'm not sure there's anything here we haven't seen in countless other spy thrillers (including, of course, the 1973 and 1997 film adaptations), but the performances and production values are top-notch, with each episode playing out like a tense mini-movie. It's been renewed for a second season. Stream The Day of the Jackal on Peacock.

Lioness is a rare Taylor Sheridan show that's not particularly related to Yellowstone, but fear not...Marshals takes us back out west and into the soothing arms of the Dutton family. Luke Grimes reprises his role as Kayce Dutton, former Livestock Agent turned...you guessed it...U.S. Marshal, protecting Montana from all manner of criminals and rustlers. The case-of-the-week format has 

The focus shifts a bit after Homeland's first few seasons, but the series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. Having been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two in the background of one of TV's most lauded spy dramas. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Priyanka Chopra stars as Alex Parrish, who graduates from the titular FBI Academy only to find herself the prime suspect in a terrorist attack on Grand Central Terminal in NYC. The show initially splits its time between Alex's quest to prove her innocence while on the run and her training days at the academy. The second season has her working for the FBI as an undercover CIA recruit (got that?) under mysterious circumstances, while the third finds her trying to bring down an international arms dealer and save a fellow agent. Stream Quantico on Hulu.

South Korean filmmaker Park Chan-wook (Decision to Leave, No Other Choice) directs this series, based, like Night Manager, on a John le Carré novel, bringing an undeniably sexy period style into the mix. Florence Pugh is Charlie, a young actress recruited by Mossad spymaster Martin Kurtz (Michael Shannon) to infiltrate a group of Palestinian terrorists, even as she's being manipulated by an Israeli intelligence officer (Alexander Skarsgård). Crucially, like the book, the show offers nuanced characters on multiple sides of the conflict, dealing more with individuals as pawns of state politicians. Buy The Little Drummer Girl from Prime Video.

Another from John le Carré, the wellspring of many modern spy sagas, so it's probably no surprise that The Night Manager (from a 1993 novel) was successful—though it certainly doesn't hurt to have a cast led by Tom Hiddleston, Hugh Laurie, and Olivia Colman. Hiddleston is Jonathan Pine, working the night shift at a luxury hotel in Switzerland when he encounters an unexpected guest: arms dealer Richard Roper (Laurie). Former Army veteran Pine had previous dealings with Roper in Cairo, and the reluctant night manager is persuaded by Foreign Office head Angela Burr (Colman) to infiltrate the criminal's organization. The first season sees Pine as a regular guy who gets involved in espionage out of near-happenstance, while the second season finds him more seasoned. A third is on the way. Stream The Night Manager on Prime Video.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings. Until...it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed and, unbeknownst to her, were also government operatives. Rescuing Rose puts Peter deep inside a web of conspiracy and official corruption. (This is why I never answer the phone.) Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

David Boreanaz is Master Chief Special Warfare Operator (a title, apparently) Jason Hayes, leader of a Navy SEAL team. There's plenty of military and undercover action of the type that you'd expect, but the show begins in the wake of the unexpected death of a team member, setting the stage for the show's unexpected emphasis on the aftermath of action, and the toll taken by service and loss on lives and families. Stream SEAL Team on Paramount+ and Netflix.

See, initially, during the 2016 Mosul Offensive, this strikingly realistic (at least, it feels that way) series drops us into the middle of an elite French special forces unit on the ground in Iraq, even though France has no official presence in the conflict. They're tasked with exfiltrating the child of a prominent IS leader, one who's offering assistance and cooperation only if the French are able to hold up their end of the bargain. For the women and men involved, it's an extremely complicated (downright messy, frankly) situation with impossible choices made by people who may or may not be making things worse. The vibe is very Hurt Locker. Stream Dark Hearts on The Roku Channel.

title: The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Is Viking Rap?
description: Catch up on the latest Gen Z and Gen A trends, from the Viking Rap AI music trends to hometown memes, clowncore, and TikTok age limits.
fullText:
This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes us from the frozen wastelands of ancient Scandinavia to Alabama courtrooms, with side quests to examine hometown nostalgia and the peculiar love Gen Z has for clowns.

The newest trend in music online is videos of Vikings rapping. Clips from fake artists with names like "Viggo Ironside" and "Ragalor" are rapidly proliferating on TikTok and other places where videos are shared. The vibe is aggressive beats and bars about Valhalla, longships, tattered flags, and wolves. The visuals are usually of muscular blonde people with tattoos in a studio doing their thing, like this:

The only other setting these Viking rappers seem to inhabit are concerts, particularly ironic given that no one will ever actually see these "artists" perform live:

The most famous Viking rapper is Draugr Balled, who was the first to really solidify the whole Viking rap genre. Balled's videos regularly earn millions of views, and you can listen to this music on legit streaming services if you want to never hang out with me.

Judging from the hundreds of comments these videos inspire ("Just wasting water," "Reposted by every 45yr old divorced dad," etc.) Kids regard Viking rap as extremely cringe, so it seems like a guilty pleasure, the kind of thing you wouldn't admit that you like, even if you secretly dig it.

For the record: Actual Vikings probably didn't have tattoos, but Viking women were generally less subjugated than women in other civilizations of the time period. Actual Vikings were also into "flyting," verse-based insult battles that seem a lot like freestyle rap battles, so there's a little historical precedent for these videos. Anyway, check out the "vikinghiphop" hashtag if you actually want to listen to more of this kind of thing. Just don't tell anyone you like it.

As I'm sure you know, a side quest in a video game is a quest that is not necessary to completing the game's main objective. In slang, a side quest is anything you do just to do it. If going to college is your quest, a side quest might be finding the underground tunnels everyone talks about, or taking an outside-your-major elective like Fencing 101 just because it looks interesting.

Big news for kids out of Alabama this week, where a court settlement may change how every kid in the U.S. uses social media. TikTok's parent company ByteDance agreed to pay Alabama over $100 million dollars to end a lawsuit claiming TikTok is designed to keep kids addicted to the platform. TikTok will also implement a two-hour daily usage limit for children, overnight and school-hour restrictions, and ban the use of cosmetic filters on kids' accounts. Underage users will also receive an interruption after 15 minutes of TikTok use, and additional pauses at 60 and 90 minutes.

While these restrictions only apply to Alabama, this is only the first state settlement of what will likely be many. There are 27 similar suits working through the court systems in other states. The likely result will be nationwide guidelines for all social media. Meta, having recently settled a federal suit, has already implemented two-hour daily time limits for young users of Facebook and Instagram and is urging it competitors to do the same. Because navigating a patchwork of state laws is not easy for tech companies, big platforms are likely to adopt the strictest state requirements as a universal standard.

I love when young people use new tools to express age-old emotions in novel ways. That's what "How I Feel in My Hometown" memes are about. You choose a fictional character, usually from an anime, to represent yourself and place 'em in scenes representing your hometown to capture that unique and melancholic sense of being a stranger in your birthplace, or having outgrown the place and seeing it with a different set of eyes. Here's an example, where Madoka Kaname contrasts with a small town:

and here's an anime character called Marin Kitagawa from My Dress-Up Darling in a Midwest town:

Another layer of irony comes from the song many memers use to accompany the video, That's My Kind of Night by Luke Bryan, an unapologetic pop-country ode to small-town life. You don't even have to know who Megumi Fushiguro from Jujutsu Kaisen is to get how he'd feel about hanging out at Texas Buc-ee's:

YouTuber BouncyClown's examination of the origin of the propeller hat "only" has about 150,000 views, so it isn't the most viral video this week, but it's a really interesting story and it's indicative of a growing trend among young people: They're really into clowns.

Clowncore is a whole thing, whether it's people doing a modern take on the "evil clown" aesthetic pioneered by the Insane Clown Posse in the last generation, kids celebrating happy clowns in general, or folks like BouncyClown who take things in a new direction by combining clown-stuff with the kind of quirky pop-culture history YouTube is known for.

To get speculative for a minute, the popularity of clowns and clowncore among young people seems like a reaction to how stultifying it is to live in a world where everyone is perfect on social media, and "cringe" is the greatest crime. It's rebellion in pancake makeup. Clowncore folks are saying, "Fuck trying to be beautiful. I'm going to make myself look as ridiculous as possible and just have fun." I'm no clown guy, but I stand behind the message 100 percent.

title: Spotify and Claude Are Both Down
description: If you can't access Spotify or Claude this morning, you're not alone.
fullText:
If you're having trouble getting your Spotify playlists up and running this morning, you're not alone. The music streaming platform is currently down for tens of thousands of users, at least. Downdetector is showing roughly 40,000 reports since 9:31 a.m. ET, with the last batch of reports coming in at 10:24 a.m. Spotify confirmed the issue in a post on X, writing: "We're aware of some issues right now and are checking them out!"

Curiously, Spotify's outage comes at the same time as an outage with Claude, the AI platform from Anthropic. Downdetector shows tens of thousands of user reports here as well, and Anthropic confirmed an ongoing issue with Claude: "We are investigating reports of degraded performance affecting claude.ai, platform.claude.com, the Claude API, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. We will provide an update as soon as possible."

It's not clear why these services are down this morning, or if they are related. But in all likelihood, Spotify and Anthropic will get their platforms back up and running soon. Typically, these occasional outages are resolved in hours, if not minutes, barring a widespread problem, like an outage with a cloud hosting provider. Last year's AWS outage "broke the internet," as did November's Cloudflare outage. There's no reason to think that's the case with these outages at this time.

title: Ulster without trio of backs for Glasgow contest
description: Ulster will be without injured backs Michael Lowry, Aitzol Arenzana-King and Robert Baloucoune for their United Rugby Championship game away to Glasgow on Saturday.
fullText:
Ulster will be without backs Michael Lowry, Aitzol Arenzana-King and Robert Baloucoune for Saturday's United Rugby Championship game against Glasgow at Scotstoun (17:30 BST).

Full-back Lowry and wing Baloucoune suffered concussions in the Irish province's 34-29 defeat by Edinburgh in their opening URC game of the 2026-27 campaign.

Winger Arenzana-King picked up a knee injury during the game in Belfast, from which Ulster emerged with two bonus points.

All three players started last weekend's fixture, with Lowry captaining the side and scoring the first of Ulster's four tries in a match which Richie Murphy's side's comeback fall short after they bounced back from a 34-5 deficit.

Glasgow began their season with an impressive 26-20 victory on the road at Munster.

"Everyone was really disappointed with how we played at the weekend but I think the glimpse of 20 minutes of really good rugby was what we were expecting to bring," Ulster head coach Richie Murphy told BBC Sport NI's Mark Sidebottom.

"Yesterday we started our review and the things that we got wrong. We know we are a lot better than that we produced at the weekend.

"This week we have a really tough assignment away to Glasgow but it's really important that we turn the page here and try and right some of the wrongs that were in that game.

"Starting with getting our breakdown right, getting our defensive line coming forward and making sure we're connected. You've got to be at your best to get anything over there."

title: Preston return 'surreal' and 'special' - Alexander
description: New Preston North End boss Graham Alexander says he feels like he has come home after returning to his old club as manager.
fullText:
New Preston North End boss Graham Alexander has said he feels like he has come home.

The 54-year-old, who made 372 league appearances for the club across two spells as a player, left League One leaders Bradford City to succeed Paul Heckingbottom at Deepdale on Monday.

Alexander has taken over a North End side that are second from bottom in the Championship with six defeats from their opening eight league games.

"Yesterday was a bit surreal - it didn't feel real until I had the training kit on," he told BBC Radio Lancashire.

"When I got home last night, me and my wife had a bit of a moment about the journey we've had to get to this point."

Alexander retired as a player with Preston at the end of the 2011-12 season aged 40, having had a brief spell as caretaker at Deepdale during that campaign.

He turned down the option to start his coaching career in the club's academy and has subsequently managed Fleetwood, Scunthorpe, Salford City, Motherwell and MK Dons.

When asked if Preston felt like home, he said: "It does yeah, it does.

"When I took the Motherwell job it was a big decision from my wife and myself to move to Scotland because we'd been so happy in Preston for 20 years but our kids were moving on.

"When we decided to move back to England, I gave my wife the choice of where she wanted to live because she'd been following me around for so long.

"The natural one was either the West Midlands, where we're both from and our families are from, or Preston and the north west area because of our relationships and how we felt here - and she chose to come back here, which I was hoping she would say.

"It's been a special place for us."

The Lilywhites return to league action after the three-week international break with a home game against Millwall on Saturday, 10 October.

Alexander, who has never managed in the Championship before, said his arrival gave the players a chance to "restart" at the club and that he was "not going to drag anything forward".

He said the extra time he will have to work with the group before a first competitive match will be important as he looks to turn their fortunes around.

"When I've took over a couple of other clubs mid-season it's been late in the week, it's been Thursday or Friday and then a game, so to have a full two weeks working with them is valuable to us but the proof will be in the pudding when we play Millwall," he said.

"It's important because there are certain things we really believe in and commit to so a two-week window to implement those things will be good but it will take longer than that to be the full team we are."

title: Keenum stars for Bears on first start since 2023
description: Veteran quarterback Case Keenum throws for two touchdowns and rushes for another as the Chicago Bears beat the Philadelphia Eagles in the NFL.
fullText:
Veteran quarterback Case Keenum starred on his first start for almost three years as the Chicago Bears handed the Philadelphia Eagles their first defeat of the season.

Starting his first NFL game since December 2023, the 38-year-old threw for 247 yards and two touchdowns and rushed for another as the Bears won 27-7 at Soldier Field in Chicago.

It is the first time he has thrown multiple touchdowns in a game since October 2019, while he is also the oldest player to score a rushing touchdown for the Bears.

Third-choice quarterback Keenum, an NFL journeyman playing at his eighth franchise, was called into action because Caleb Williams suffered a hamstring injury last week and his back-up Tyson Bagent then suffered a concussion.

Wide receiver Kalif Raymond, who scored a touchdown, said: "He was like, 'I may not be a cowboy, but this is definitely not my first rodeo'. [There's] a lot of confidence in him; a lot of confidence in himself.

"He practises, preps every week, but particularly this week. We didn't expect anything different from him."

Keenum's first drive resulted in a touchdown for Luther Burden III, and Cairo Santos added a 29-yard field goal before Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts rushed for a touchdown to cut the Bears' half-time lead to 10-7.

Santos added a second field goal early in the third quarter before the Bears scored two touchdowns among 17 unanswered points.

The Bears defence limited the Eagles to 248 total yards and claimed two interceptions - one from Jalen Hurts and another from his back-up Andy Dalton, who came in for four snaps while Hurts was checked for a potential concussion in the second quarter.
