title: Aston Villa sack boss Arroyo after winless WSL start
description: Aston Villa manager Natalia Arroyo is sacked following two defeats and two draws in their opening four matches of the Women's Super League season.
fullText:
Aston Villa manager Natalia Arroyo has been sacked following a disappointing start to the Women's Super League season.

Villa are yet to win this season, drawing two and losing two of their opening four matches and BBC Sport is told that led to the club’s decision.

They suffered a 4-0 defeat by Tottenham on Sunday in the WSL and are due to play Newcastle in the Women's League Cup on Wednesday (19:30 BST).

Spaniard Arroyo joined Villa in January 2025 and had another two years remaining on her contract.

She becomes the first managerial departure this season, though former Manchester United boss Marc Skinner and ex-Brighton head coach Dario Vidosic both stepped down earlier this year.

The club informed Arroyo of their decision on Monday evening and players were told on Tuesday morning.

Former Everton manager Brian Sorensen, who is now Villa’s women’s technical advisor, has been placed in interim charge.

Since Arroyo's arrival, Villa have shown flashes of potential and she initially steadied the ship as they toyed with relegation in her first six months at the club.

But despite investment in the transfer window, Villa lacked consistency and were underwhelming last season.

There was pressure on them to perform in 2026-27 and while they earned a draw on the opening weekend against Chelsea, they have looked dangerously open at the back and chaotic out of possession.

Their latest defeat by Spurs was a worrying display and appears to have been enough to lead to Arroyo's sacking.

title: Does Horner have a chance of Ferrari job? F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
fullText:
Mercedes' George Russell took his first victory since June by holding off Max Verstappen to win the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Verstappen's Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar completed the podium on his return after missing three races with a broken wrist.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli finished fifth in Baku, meaning his advantage over team-mate Russell has narrowed to 66 points.

This weekend, Formula 1 heads to Malaysia, the host of the Bahrain Grand Prix - an event originally due to take place in April but which was postponed because of the war in the Middle East.

Before the race in Sepang, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Does Christian Horner really want the team principal job at Ferrari, or even have a shot at it? - Ben

This topic has become a subject for conversation in recent days following an interview Horner did with the Times, external as he promotes his new book.

Horner said: "At this stage in my life, there's only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership."

Asked whether he would take a job there, he replied: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1."

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur made his views about Horner's intervention pretty plain after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix when he said: "Mr Horner is looking for a job - that, everybody knows - everywhere."

Vasseur said the speculation surrounding the team meant Ferrari were "not working in the perfect serenity".

Horner's comments seem to make it clear that he would consider a job offer from Ferrari. But the key questions are under what conditions he might accept it, and whether he would be offered it in the first place.

Horner has made it very clear over the years that he believes an F1 team needs one person in charge and in overall control.

It's highly unlikely he would get that at Ferrari, where chairman John Elkann and chief executive officer Benedetto Vigna will always have more authority than any team principal.

Even at Red Bull, where Horner had theoretical leadership at the F1 team, he was ultimately answerable to headquarters in Austria and that is what led to his removal in the end.

It's hard to imagine how Elkann and Vigna could or would countenance any situation where they were removed from any input into the F1 team.

And it's even harder to imagine a situation where that was not the de facto position even if a team boss had been given assurances they would be left alone.

Then there is the question of whether Ferrari would want Horner.

Horner comes with baggage. All of the above for a start, and on top of that there is the cloud under which he left Red Bull.

There is no doubt that he was a remarkably successful team principal there, the team winning eight drivers' titles, six constructors' championships and 124 grands prix in his two-decade tenure.

However, the team unravelled in his final 18 months in charge, in the wake of the accusations of sexual harassment and coercive, controlling behaviour that were made against him by a female employee.

Red Bull dismissed those allegations after two internal investigations led by external lawyers.

But they were a key factor in Adrian Newey leaving his position as chief technical officer - along with internal politics in which Newey felt his role had been diminished by Horner.

Newey was followed out of the door by long-time sporting director Jonathan Wheatley and head of strategy Will Courtenay.

Horner was finally dismissed following a slump in form which Red Bull bosses concluded the team did not appear to be capable of arresting under his leadership.

In the Times interview, Horner says that the only justification he was given by Red Bull for his sacking was "it was more Christian Horner Racing than Red Bull Racing".

He adds at other points in the interview: "I am a bit of a Marmite character. I know I'm not everybody's cup of tea. It's impossible to be." And: "I'm the cure and the problem."

Clearly, any decision as to whether Horner is the person you want to lead your F1 team would need careful consideration.

It's also worth mentioning that Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton has made it pretty clear over the past few years that he has little time for Horner.

'I still feel as fast as anybody' - Alonso on why he's staying in F1

Why hasn't the FIA made a decision on the final two races of the season? They've cancelled the final rounds of the World Rally Championship and World Endurance Championship because of the Middle East conflict. Surely they should be confirming the changes in the calendar now? - Nigel

To start with a point of order, it is Formula 1 that decides the calendar - as in, the commercial rights holder - not the FIA, the governing body. The FIA's role is effectively only to rubber-stamp F1's decision.

As things stand, F1 is planning to end the season as the calendar was originally scheduled - with Las Vegas followed by Qatar and then Abu Dhabi, external over the last two weekends in November and the first in December.

Although the war continues between the US/Israel and Iran, the advice F1 has been getting is that the situation in those two countries is stable, and there is not a high risk of attacks on civilian infrastructure.

The UK Foreign Office, for example, does not advise against travel to Qatar and Abu Dhabi., external It simply says the situation there "remains unpredictable" and that "there is a risk of more attacks and unforeseen escalation in the region".

And the two countries consider themselves open for business.

However, F1 has a contingency plan.

Imola in Italy is preparing to host a race on the weekend of Abu Dhabi.

If the two Middle Eastern races cannot happen as a result of an escalation of the situation in the Gulf, Imola would step in and hold the season finale on 4-6 December.

But unless and until that happens, there is no confirmation of changes to make, as there are currently no changes.

Why wasn't a virtual safety car called when Valtteri Bottas crashed right at the end in Azerbaijan? This was obviously a dangerous situation as the car was buried in the barrier. And it almost cost George Russell a well-deserved victory - Steve

Valtteri Bottas crashed at Turn 15 on the penultimate lap of the race, meaning his Cadillac was in the barriers there when leaders George Russell and Max Verstappen came around their last lap less than a second apart.

Normally, a car in the barriers on a street circuit means at least a virtual safety car.

However, in this instance a spokesperson for governing body the FIA says that race control "determined that it was safe to let the leaders race to the line - they were able to cut the apex at T15, as it's a relatively slow corner".

In the event, the Bottas incident, the FIA says, was "successfully managed by localised double yellows".

Whether this was the correct course of action, and whether the decision was influenced by wanting to prevent the grand prix finishing under caution, will remain a subject for debate.

On the one hand, it allowed the race to continue and be exciting to the end.

On the other, slowing for the incident caused a technical issue for Russell's Mercedes.

"I lifted off the power and when I went back, I had no turbo, so then I had no power," Russell said. "Max almost got me at the line."

Russell was able to mitigate this loss of power from the internal combustion engine because, it being the final lap, he could use up all his battery on the run to the flag, rather than have to keep it balanced for the following lap.

So he managed to hang on - but by less than 0.2 seconds.

Had he not, the decision by race control would have come under a great deal more scrutiny than it did.

I love your explainers. Please can you analyse the data explaining the jump Williams have made with their upgrades. It seems more significant than Aston Martin's much written-about 'leap'? What are the percentages, averages etc. - John

First of all, thanks very much for the compliment.

This is a complex topic. There is no doubt that the lighter chassis and aerodynamic upgrades introduced by Williams in Baku marked a step forward.

It was their best qualifying performance of the year in terms of positions, even if in percentage terms they were actually slightly closer to the front in Miami back in May.

But it's too early to judge the Williams upgrades - and Aston Martin provides a clue as to why.

This year, there is quite a swing in competitiveness for certain teams depending on circuit type.

Regardless of the upgrades, Williams always expected Baku to be one of their stronger circuits - short-duration corners and long straights suit their car.

But they struggle in long-duration corners, so it will be interesting to see how they go this weekend in Malaysia, because Sepang is full of them.

Likewise, Aston Martin have specific weaknesses.

Their aerodynamic upgrade in Hungary improved their chassis performance by in the region of two seconds a lap.

Hence their significant improvement there and in Zandvoort, where Fernando Alonso drove superbly to take two points for ninth place.

But, despite its upgrade for Zandvoort, the Honda engine remains the worst on the grid, in terms of overall power, driveability and energy management.

So, it's no surprise that on two hugely engine-dependent circuits such as Monza and Baku, they would struggle.

On that basis, Aston Martin can be expected to be relatively more competitive again in Singapore, with its low power-sensitivity, and where Alonso is usually outstanding.

title: Barney's Bears - the Warwickshire captain who commands respect
description: How Shropshire lad Ed Barnard skippered Warwickshire to a title triumph in his first season as a county captain.
fullText:
Behind every great team there is generally a great leader and Warwickshire's County Championship winning captain Ed Barnard is the latest to fit that particular bill.

To take over as skipper just a fortnight before the start of a new season, then lead your team to the Championship is the stuff of dreams.

For Barney's Bears to do it in the manner they did, winning their final four games, three of them by an innings, makes the 2026 title race take on even more legendary status.

From the moment red-ball cricket returned in August, Warwickshire won five matches and drew the other.

The first of those victories, a desperately tense one-wicket win over Sussex marshalled by last pair Chris Woakes and Olly Hannon-Dalby, was probably the one inspirational trigger point of the Bears' charge to the title.

But the coolest man on and off the field as the drama hotted up was 30-year-old Barnard, the Shropshire-born former Worcestershire all-rounder, who swapped the Pears for the Bears at the end of the 2022 season.

"He's just so consistent both as a player and a person," Warwickshire first-team coach Ian Westwood told BBC Radio WM.

"He's made my job so simple this year, with the high standards he sets and the way he leads from the front with bat and ball. He commands the respect of everyone in he changing room because of who he is."

Bears beat Leicestershire to secure ninth title

The Bears' necessity: Just how good is top wicket-taker Bamber?

There was also a lovely irony that, having won his only previous trophy as a Worcestershire player in 2018 - the T20 Blast - in beating Leicestershire last weekend, also at Edgbaston, Barnard was again in the company of the Pears' dual matchwinner that day, Ben Cox, now the Foxes wicketkeeper. A pair of once young tyros now all grown up!

The crucial run of four straight wins in September, also at Southampton, Cardiff and Chelmsford, was what catapulted Warwickshire from outsiders to a ninth title.

"Over the last month we've been exceptional," added Westwood.

"It seemed a long time to wait from winning at Chelmsford to getting the last game started and, when it became ours to lose, it added to the pressure. But Ed and the lads dealt with it all superbly."

Westwood - a Warwickshire title winner himself in 2012 - also acknowledges the part played by returning bowling coach Graeme 'Pop' Welch and Sussex-bound batting coach Matthew Walker.

"The bowling has got lots of plaudits and rightly so. Ethan Bamber, Woakesey [Chris Woakes] and Olly [Hannon-Dalby] have been brilliant and Manny Suthar has come in and given us just what we need," Westwood said.

"But we've done really well with the bat. We've played on a lot of bowler-friendly pitches and still scored the runs we needed."

All spearheaded by 1,048 runs from Sam Hain, at a stunning average of almost 75, a genuine beacon of consistency as he passed 50 in 10 of his 13 matches (two tons and eight half-centuries).

"Sam Hain has been like a man possessed," said Westwood. "He's the leader of that batting group. We couldn't have done it without him."

Barnard managed one unprecedented achievement when he lifted the trophy on Saturday afternoon - he became the first cricketer from Shropshire to do it.

Plenty of Shropshire-born players have gone on to enjoy good first-class careers.

One of them, Oswestry's Andy Lloyd, even opened the batting for England. Both Barnard and Joe Clarke played for England at Under-19 and Lions level before becoming sidelined, for differing reasons.

But then Barnard is from particularly strong Minor Counties-bred stock.

Not only was he born in a Minor County, in the county town Shrewsbury, his elder brother Mike also played for Shropshire and they were the sons of a Minor Counties player.

Their father, Andy, held a coaching role both at Shrewsbury Cricket Club and in the cricket academy at Shrewsbury School under former Worcestershire paceman Paul Pridgeon - the latter a production line that has also churned out the likes of James Taylor, Joe Leach, Issy Wong and Dillon Pennington.

Barnard Snr was also part of the most famous day in the county's cricketing history back in 1984, when he took the last three wickets as Shropshire famously turned over mighty Yorkshire, starring Geoffrey Boycott (c & b Brian Perry 27, for the record), in the first round of the NatWest Trophy.

Now Barnard Jr's efforts this summer have helped put Proud Salopia right back on the cricket map.

title: How Manzambi became one of Europe's best young talents
description: Aston Villa's summer signing Johan Manzambi has been nominated for the best young player at the Ballon d'Or ceremony. BBC Sport looks at his rise.
fullText:
In just two years Johan Manzambi has gone from being an unknown teenager to a European star.

The 20-year-old could be named young talent of the year at the Ballon d'Or ceremony next month having only made his senior debut for Freiburg in 2024.

A breakout season in Germany last term convinced Villa to pay more than £50m for a player with just 47 club starts.

Manzambi scored on his full Villa debut to help secure a first Premier League win of the season and now faces Scotland with Switzerland in the Nations League on Tuesday looking to continue his progression.

Life bright for Gilmour after baseball and World Cup heartache

Vega hails Yakin and Manzambi as Swiss head for Hampden

Manzambi is already in the discussion with fellow nominees Lamine Yamal of Barcelona, Real Madrid's Yan Diomande and new Manchester City midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi for the best young player in the world award.

He scored three goals in four games for Switzerland at the World Cup before a knee injury ended his tournament, only a year after making his full international debut.

It is a rapid rise for a player who used to return to Freiburg's academy to do his washing.

Bernhard Weis, who gave Manzambi his debut for Freiburg Under-19s, told BBC Sport: "He is playing for the professionals and he comes to us at the academy and brings some dirty clothes.

"He didn't have a washing machine so he comes here and washes some clothes.

"I would speak with him and then he would pick up some young guys from the under-13s, under-14s and take them to the train station.

"He would see the guys and say, 'come with me, I'll take you to the station', so they could get home. That's Johan Manzambi."

As for his profile, though, Weis did not expect a Ballon d'Or nomination coming so quickly.

He added: "I didn't see that. I saw something for the first team, for us, but this way, no chance.

"The first half year at Freiburg it was not so easy for him, he's not so strong and he's not so stable. He put on five kilos and then he thought, 'now I go, it's the right moment, I will be faster and stronger'.

Massimo Lombardo, Servette's academy director agreed. He first worked with Manzambi when he was 15 and oversaw his early development before he moved to Freiburg as a 17-year-old in 2023.

"It is a real surprise for many people, that he can do something special so quickly," he told BBC Sport.

"For me, the difference he can make is because of his mentality, personality, enthusiasm and courage. He has the technical skills and tactical skills and the physical possibility now to perform in England.

Why Newcastle target Manzambi is in demand

"Mentally he was always a player who, when he came into the training session and games, always wanted to do something important. You can see that as a player who starts with Freiburg, he took his chance.

"I can remember his second game with Switzerland, against the USA and he scored. It was always important for him to come into the game and to do something."

Last season Manzambi was named the Europa League's Young Player of the Season, as Freiburg lost the final to Villa in May.

He scored 12 goals in 61 appearances and Weis, now Freiburg II boss, has watched him develop, with Manzambi also learning German in three months.

It helped him swiftly move from the academy to the first team, making his debut against Heidenheim a year after joining.

Weis described him a "difference maker" and, among players in the Bundesliga in his position last season, Manzambi ranked first for 10-plus metre progressive carries (116), shot-ending carries (13) and fouls won (78).

Villa knew he would move this summer so it was a case of now or never for Emery. Had he gone to Newcastle instead they believed his next move would put him out of their financial reach.

The Magpies were always wary of being hijacked, having previously lost Victor Munoz to Liverpool and, while they agreed a deal with Freiburg, they never got a yes from Manzambi.

Villa then turned the versatile forward into the most expensive Swiss player in history - surpassing Granit Xhaka's £38.25m move from Borussia Mönchengladbach to Arsenal 10 years ago.

Yet, despite signing a five-year deal, Weis backed him to make the next step quickly.

"I think Aston Villa is the right club for him. He will play every time when he is fit and that's the right way. Then I think he plays two seasons at Villa and then he goes to the next step," he added.

"After the World Cup I said he must go to the Premier League. Bayern Munich were mentioned, he didn't go to [Borussia] Dortmund, [Bayer] Leverkusen. It's the right way."

Freiburg have made light of Manzambi's absence and went into the international break unbeaten and sitting third, having topped the Bundesliga after three straight opening wins.

Without him they have won six of their seven games in all competitions, scoring 24 goals, and boss Julian Schuster said earlier this month he had hoped to keep the player.

It was the same for Lombardo at Servette, who fought to keep their young talent, but the former Switzerland international admitted Manzambi had made the right decisions.

"We wanted him to stay with us, we gave him a contract but he wouldn't sign and history would say it's a good way, he came to Freiburg and played with the under-19s and was always improving," said the ex-Perugia midfielder.

"Then Johan came into the first team and performed so well he started to play from the beginning and the coach couldn't move him from the starting XI.

"With us he was incredible, he wanted to stay on the pitch to improve, to stay in the games and he had a lot of personality at 15. You can see into a group of young players who has the personality to speak.

"He has a lot of personality. Other players were stronger and quicker but he trained with enthusiasm and I saw a young player who wanted to do something special."

title: Czech Republic ready for Wembley 30 years after Euro '96
description: The Czech Republic are returning to Wembley for a Nations League game with England, just over 30 years after their Euro '96 heartbreak there.
fullText:
The Czech Republic will return to the north London site that staged one of the biggest days in their history during this international break - as they head back to Wembley.

They face England twice in Nations League Group A3 - in Prague on Tuesday (19:45 BST) and London on 6 October.

The Czechs have been to Wembley since losing the Euro '96 final to Germany under the old stadium's twin towers, but this visit marks the 30-year anniversary of that remarkable summer in England.

Euro '96 was the first European Championship staged after Czechoslovakia separated - forming the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

But nobody expected the Czech team to have much impact at the tournament, including the country's own players.

They were outsiders, and most of the squad were still based in their domestic league.

Several had booked their holidays for straight after the group stage - which involved Germany, Italy and Russia - and Vladimir Smicer was even due to get married.

Midfielder Patrik Berger says his then Borussia Dortmund team-mate Jurgen Kohler did not even know the Czechs were at the Euros... and the defender was in the Germany squad.

Berger, speaking to the BBC Sporting Witness podcast earlier this year, said of Kohler: "He was asking me what my plans were for the summer. I said 'I'm going to the Euros' and he said 'to watch games?'

"I said 'no, we're playing you guys the first game of the group stages and then we will play in the final' - and he was laughing."

The Czechs lost their opening game 2-0 to Germany at Old Trafford before beating Italy 2-1 at Anfield.

Smicer's late equaliser in a 3-3 draw against Russia - at his future home of Anfield - was enough to see them through because Italy failed to beat Germany in the other game, finishing 0-0.

"We knew we were still in it, but we didn't know what the other result is," said Berger, who would go on to play for Liverpool with Smicer. "One minute we're not qualifying, the next it was we qualified, so we didn't really know.

"After the final whistle it took a few minutes before we realised we qualified for the quarter-finals."

In the quarters came one of the most memorable European Championship goals ever, with Karel Poborsky scooping the ball over Vitor Baia from the edge of the box to give the Czech Republic a 1-0 win over Portugal at Villa Park.

And, after a goalless draw against France in the semis at Old Trafford, the Czechs would win 6-5 on penalties.

Their spot-kicks were netted by players including future Ballon d'Or winner Pavel Nedved, Berger and Poborsky, who was back at the ground weeks later as a newly signed Manchester United player.

"You don't want to go there," said Berger of taking a penalty in a shootout.

"If someone says something different they're lying. Nobody wants to take that penalty."

He said the team "couldn't believe" they had beaten France.

"We were living the dream," Berger said. "It was an amazing feeling. An amazing moment for the country.

"To get to the final was kind of like a miracle for everyone."

Two days before the final, Smicer returned to Prague to get married.

Thousands of Czech fans turned out in the city centre for the occasion, but Smicer had to return to England the same day.

The Czech Republic faced Germany in the final at Wembley - and led after 59 minutes through Berger's drilled penalty.

He revealed he was not even meant to be the penalty taker but "could see nobody really wanted to take the ball".

"The only thing in my mind was hit it as hard as possible on target," he said.

Sadly for the Czechs, Oliver Bierhoff equalised 14 minutes later - and then scored the first ever golden goal in a major tournament final to give Germany the win.

"It wasn't meant to be," said Berger. "I'd love to be European champion, but silver for us was like a gold because it opened doors to so many of us. And it opened doors to the generation after us. I have no regrets.

"Thanks to Euro 96, because it was played in England, I caught the eye of Liverpool.

"There were 100,000 waiting for us in Prague celebrating. Even silver felt like winning the tournament for us."

As Czechoslovakia, the country won the European Championship in 1976 - and lost two World Cup finals (1934 and 1962).

But the Czech Republic's first tournament as a separate nation remains the last time they reached a final.

They have, however, enjoyed other memorable European Championships - having reached the 2004 semi-finals and the quarters in 2012 and 2021.

The 2004 squad had a mix of youth - such as Petr Cech, Milan Baros and Tomas Rosicky - and experience with Smicer, Berger and Poborsky.

They lost to eventual winners Greece in the last four.

Ondrej Zlamal, a Prague-based football journalist, says that team and their performances "were even better" than in 1996.

"This generation with Nedved and others culminated in 2004 and we had a feeling we should have won the Euros. We played better football than in 1996," Zlamal said. "It was the second highlight of the golden generation."

Their only two World Cups since then - 2006 and 2026 - have ended in group stage exits.

Zlamal said: "The performance this summer was really disappointing.

"There is a simple answer to why [the team have not lived up to the heights of the past] – we don't have such talented footballers as we had.

"We don't have enough players in the top teams like we used to.

"When I was six I watched the 1976 final which Czechoslovakia won, and my father told me 'remember this because you won't see it any more'.

"I don't believe this generation can reach such a success because the competition and football is much bigger.

"Miracles happen and maybe there could be a new generation which could be surprising as 1996... but I don't believe it will happen again."

A new era is starting with the Czech team under Spaniard Santi Denia, the first foreign manager in the national side's history.

His first squad - for Nations League games against Croatia, England and Spain - contains seven players with either no caps or one cap - although none are aged under 22.

Thirty years since Berger, Smicer, Poborsky and Nedved endured their north London heartbreak, the creaking old stadium has long ago been substituted out and replaced by a Wembley fit for the 21st Century.

Denia and his players could certainly pick a worse setting to deliver a statement performance.

title: Red Roses to return to Sunderland for Women's Six Nations
description: England will return to Sunderland's Stadium of Light – the venue for their record-breaking Women's Rugby World Cup opener – for the 2027 Six Nations.
fullText:
England will return to Sunderland's Stadium of Light - the venue for their record-breaking Women's Rugby World Cup opener - in their first home match of the 2027 Six Nations.

The Red Roses will play Scotland at the venue on 17 April.

It will be the first time they have played a home match away from a rugby-specific ground outside of a World Cup.

England drew 42,723 fans to the Stadium of Light for the 67-9 victory over the United States that opened the Women's Rugby World Cup in August 2025.

That attendance surpassed the 42,579 who watched the final of the previous edition as the Women's Rugby World Cup's biggest crowd.

The Red Roses subsequently smashed that mark again with an 81,885 sell-out for their final victory over Canada at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium.

England's 2027 Six Nations campaign also includes home matches against Italy at Northampton's DPD Stadium at Franklin's Gardens on 24 April and a final-round meeting against France at Twickenham on 15 May.

The venues for their away fixtures against Wales and Ireland are yet to be announced

"It was an amazing atmosphere to be a part of - one of the favourites in my career," England full-back Ellie Kildunne said of her previous visit to the Stadium of Light.

"I just remember the noise when we got off the bus and the amount of time the fans stayed behind afterwards. It was incredible. They really spurred us on that night.

"If the match with Scotland can replicate anything close to that night, it's sure to be another memorable occasion."

England are aiming for their ninth successive Six Nations crown.

Their preparations for the tournament will begin after they play two Tests against Canada and one Test against the United States on the away leg of their WXV Global Series campaign next month.

title: Inside Liverpool's increasing global investment in youth
description: Liverpool are becoming increasingly proactive in their search for global young talent. BBC Sport takes a closer look.
fullText:
Liverpool may have made three signings worth more than £100m each over the past two summers in Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola, but internally there is a realisation that after a significant amount of young talent was sold last summer, the club need to replenish that talent pool.

Since 2020, Liverpool have made more than £230m from selling players who have represented them at youth level and that has been a major part of owner Fenway Sports Group's self-sustaining business model, with the funds reinvested into the club.

Since Brexit, there is a 'premium' on young English players and it is why Liverpool's global talent department, led by Matt Newberry since the winter of 2024, now have a major role to play.

Fifa rules state that international transfers of players are only permitted if the player is over 18 and, since Brexit, Premier League clubs are no longer permitted to sign players under 18 from European countries.

Newberry's team is responsible for deciding which young talents from overseas should be targeted for a move. Using their wealth of contacts across the world, including dedicated regional scouts, Liverpool are becoming increasingly aggressive in the space.

It helps that new sporting director Julian Ward is well known for his global network.

"Any player we sign, the first intention is that we want them to play in the first team and there's a belief that there's a chance for everyone that signs here," Alex Inglethorpe, Liverpool Academy director told BBC Sport.

"That really is no different since the impact of Brexit on the English market, which is quite significant. There's now a premium on young English players. Time will tell if that premium is worthwhile but it's definitely a change.

"So it's fairly natural for a club like Liverpool to look within Merseyside in the first instance then broaden that out - national recruitment happens at 14 and after that you look globally, which is what we've done."

Mor Talla Ndiaye's journey began in the Senegalese village of Sandiara where he played football in the streets.

He progressed through the ranks playing for Bousports Academy in the town of Thiadiaye before joining Amitie Football Club in the city of Thies.

Come January this year, Liverpool fended off interest from other European clubs and signed the 18-year-old for about £1m plus add-ons.

"You have access to certain talent based on points accrued from playing homegrown players. We had a couple of ESC (elite significant contribution) spots to explore the wider market and that's something which, even prior to Brexit, was a fairly normal thing," Inglethorpe adds.

Ndiaye is a left-footed centre-half who played for Liverpool in pre-season under Andoni Iraola and was an unused substitute in three games in the second half of last season under Arne Slot.

"He's an incredible story, isn't he? From where he's come from to where he is - and he's such a humble kid. He's an unbelievable lad to work with," Rob Page, Liverpool's U21 boss, told BBC Sport.

"There's exciting times ahead but he's got a lot of work to do. He's nowhere near the finished article but he's on the right path. His attitude is spot on and he's at the club that will definitely help him develop."

At Liverpool, there is an optimism regarding Ndiaye and a genuine belief that if he makes it to the top, it could be one of the great football stories.

Liverpool opened discussions with his academy and his agency, Sport Cover, after scouts spotted his performances at the U17 World Cup in Qatar last winter and several video calls were arranged before the club's representatives travelled to Senegal.

Once there, they visited where Ndiaye trained, as well as meeting the people that supported his development before presenting their vision to him directly.

A round-table meeting was organised with his family to help understand his environment, the story and the context in which he grew up.

Ultimately, Ndiaye chose Liverpool because they offered the clearest pathway and their approach in getting to know him stood out.

Ndiaye isn't the only player to have been identified and recruited by Liverpool's global talent team.

After the U17 World Cup, Liverpool also made a £2.6m move for another centre-half, Ifeanyi Ndukwe.

Ndukwe was impressive in pre-season and the 18-year-old Austrian has gone on loan to Levante in La Liga as he looks to obtain a UK work permit.

The list doesn't stop there. Samuel Martinez, the 17-year-old Colombian midfielder, will join next summer after having "30 offers from around the world, external", according to his father.

It doesn't always work. Arsenal beat Liverpool to the signing of Andria Bartishvili from Georgia last month and the 17-year-old will join the Gunners next summer when he is 18.

But the moves for Martinez and Ndiaye showcase Liverpool's willingness to spread beyond Europe and into areas they may not have explored before. Given the inevitability of other top clubs circling emerging talent, the idea of selling the pathway that Liverpool offers is imperative.

Since arriving, Ndiaye has settled in with a host family - which is normal when players aren't from the area - that are used to working with Liverpool.

"Players come from varying parts of the world and, when someone comes in and doesn't speak much English at the start, you have to help with that and help understand culturally the differences in food, the weather and even the pitches you play on," Inglethorpe said.

"There's a lot of understanding in terms of the level of support that's needed and the most important thing you can give a young player is the time.

"I'm delighted that Mor made such a strong impression and he's done as well as he has, but we hope that he's going to get better and better as he continues to adapt."

This summer, Liverpool also confirmed moves for Lucca Brughmans, the 18-year-old Belgian goalkeeper, and Djylian N'Guessan, the 18-year-old French forward, with both set to join the club permanently in 2027.

In the modern game, most talents are known and there aren't many hidden gems anymore, but Liverpool believe that by digging deeper and wider they can get ahead of the curve, using their global network and their reputation as a club that will help players develop.

title: Top 14 award winner Willis reiterates desire to play Test rugby
description: Jack Willis, who last played for England at the 2023 Rugby World Cup,  retains his award as the best player in France.
fullText:
Jack Willis, who last played for England at the 2023 Rugby World Cup, jokingly challenged reporters to find him a way back into Test rugby after he retained his award as the best player in France.

Willis moved to Toulouse in November 2022 after Wasps went out of business, and was initially given dispensation to continue playing for England given the exceptional circumstances.

The back row won the most recent of his 14 caps in a pool-stage hammering of Chile, but, having opted to remain in French club rugby, has not been eligible for England since.

A long-standing policy restricts England selection to domestic-based players. It strengthens Prem clubs' ability to retain top talent, while England also benefit from increased access and control over their players.

Willis has been a huge success across the Channel. He was named player of the match in June's Top14 final win over Montpellier as he added a fourth French title to the Champions Cup crown he lifted in 2024.

Willis came top of a three-man shortlist for the Top14's best player for the 2025-26 campaign, seeing off competition from France and Bordeaux-Begles fly-half Matthieu Jalibert and Clermont-Auvergne's All Black Harry Plummer.

Willis becomes only the second player - after France captain Antoine Dupont - to retain the accolade.

The 29-year-old made his decision to stay at Toulouse, where his contract runs until 2029, despite knowing it would put him out of contention for an England spot.

"You know what you sacrifice," Willis said of his Test career.

"It's something I still want to do, but rules are rules."

Willis is now, in theory, available for selection by Ireland.

Three years have passed since he last appeared for England and, under World Rugby's 'birthright' rule, he could now represent a country which he, his parents or his grandparents were born in. Willis' grandfather was born in Belfast.

Ireland's strong preference for home-based players has been relaxed on rare occasions in the past with Jonny Sexton and Tommy Bowe continuing to play for their country despite moves to Racing 92 and the Ospreys respectively.

However, the likes of Simon Zebo have also found themselves excluded after heading overseas.

It is highly unlikely any compromise would be found that allows Willis to play for Ireland while remaining with Toulouse.

"I'm a quarter Irish, but they have the same rules as England," said Willis.

"You need to do some digging, that's your job, you find the way [around the rules]!"

title: Taylor to come out of retirement and reunite with Lewis
description: Phil Taylor will come out of retirement to play in the Modus Super Series alongside Adrian Lewis in November.
fullText:
Sixteen-time world champion Phil Taylor will return to darts eight years after retiring to play in the Modus Super Series' International Pairs tournament in November.

Taylor will play alongside another former world champion, Adrian Lewis, who himself has not played professionally on the PDC circuit since April 2023.

Taylor, 66, is the most-decorated player in the sport's history. 'The Power' won 214 professional tournaments and a record 87 major tournaments between 1987 and 2018.

The doubles tournament takes place between 23 and 28 November in Portsmouth.

Nicknamed 'Jackpot', 41-year-old Lewis won the World Darts Championship in 2011 and 2012 and has faced Taylor in five Professional Darts Corporation major title finals, all of which were won by Taylor.

The duo are the most successful pairing in the history of the PDC's World Cup of Darts, winning it four times as Team England in their six outings together.

"I've been asked plenty of times about coming back, but it would have to be for the right reason," said Taylor.

"Adrian is one of the very few people I'd come out of retirement to play alongside, and the Modus Super Series is the place I wanted to do it.

"We've got a lot of history together, we know each other's games inside out and I'm looking forward to getting back up there with him."

While Taylor has not played professionally since 2018, he did feature at the World Seniors Darts Championship in 2022, 2023 and 2024.

Lewis featured at Modus' International Pairs Tournament for England last year alongside Steve Beaton, having announced he was taking a break from darts in April 2023.

"Phil and I have shared some brilliant moments playing together over the years, so to get the chance to do it again is really special," said Lewis.

"We know what it takes to win as a pair and I'm looking forward to seeing what we can do together."

title: Ferrari back Vasseur amid speculation over future
description: Ferrari back Frederic Vasseur as their F1 team principal after former Red Bull boss Christian Horner says he would be interested in joining.
fullText:
Ferrari have backed Frederic Vasseur as their Formula 1 team principal.

The official statement comes amid speculation over the Frenchman's position, fuelled by former Red Bull team principal Christian Horner saying he would be interested, external in joining Ferrari.

Ferrari chief communication officer Maria Conti used a hastily convened media call to deliver the message, saying she was speaking on behalf of chairman John Elkann and chief executive officer Benedetto Vigna.

"Ferrari's position is clear," Conti said. "It will not change. l am officially saying - I don't have John here with me, but Ferrari has made its choice. There is confidence in Fred and his team. Nothing has changed."

Does Horner have a chance of Ferrari job? F1 Q&A

Horner a distraction for Ferrari, says Vasseur

Ferrari entered the 2026 season hoping their preparations for widespread rule changes covering cars and engines would give them a chance to become championship contenders.

But, although their chassis started the season regarded as the best in F1, their engine has fallen short of the performance set by Mercedes and Red Bull.

Ferrari are second in the constructors' championship after 15 of a scheduled 23 races, but a massive 160 points behind leaders Mercedes and more concerned about fending off a challenge from McLaren, who are 72 points adrift in third place.

On Saturday after the race Lewis Hamilton was asked whether he was still confident Ferrari were heading in the right direction under Vasseur. He replied: "Yes."

Vasseur said after the race in Baku in reference to speculation about his future: "We are not working in the perfect serenity. For me, first, but for everybody in the team, for the media, for 50% of the questions [to be] about this, it's a bit of a frustrating situation.

"We are fighting for P2 in the championship, and at the end of the day we are all speaking a lot about this, and even for the guys in the garage, to discuss about this, it's the best discussion that we can have.

"But it is what it is - it's not in my hands. Mr Horner is looking for a job - that everybody knows - everywhere.

"But what can I do? Just try to do my best to push the team, to rise them to be motivated."

Vasseur signed a new contract with Ferrari in July last year. Ferrari did not say how long it lasted beyond describing it as "a multi-year contract for the coming Formula 1 seasons".

Vasseur joined Ferrari at the start of 2023 after former team principal Mattia Binotto was removed following a bright start to the previous regulation set in 2022 was followed by a slump marked by poor reliability and questionable operational decisions.

title: Ex-England captain Dallaglio to sell World Cup winner's medal
description: Former England captain Lawrence Dallaglio is set to sell his 2003 Rugby World Cup winner's medal after being declared bankrupt.
fullText:
Former England captain Lawrence Dallaglio is set to sell his 2003 Rugby World Cup winner's medal after being declared bankrupt.

The 54-year-old has put a number of items from his illustrious career up for auction including medals, trophies and caps.

The World Cup medal is expected to raise between £50,000 and £80,000 while in total the collection has an estimated value of £180,000.

Dallaglio was one of the stars of the England side that won the World Cup in dramatic fashion against Australia 23 years ago.

Other items up for sale include a British and Irish Lions cap, his 1993 World Cup Sevens winner's medal and a 2003 Six Nations Championship winner's medal.

During an appearance on The High Performance podcast, external earlier this month, Dallaglio spoke about his bankrupcy.

He said: "As a result of getting divorced, I was made bankrupt.

"I had some financial problems - I could've done things a lot better."

He also said he sought therapy after his divorce and bankruptcy left him wallowing in "self-pity".

The auction at Budd's, external in Northamptonshire takes place on 13 October.

title: 'I still feel as fast as anybody' - Alonso on why he's staying in F1
description: Fernando Alonso commits to staying in Formula 1 with Aston Martin for at least one more year. - and explains why to BBC Sport.
fullText:
Fernando Alonso has committed to staying in Formula 1 with Aston Martin for at least one more year - and says the biggest single reason for his decision is because he "still feels fast".

The 45-year-old Spaniard has been weighing up his future all year. And while, like Max Verstappen, he has been outspoken in his criticism of the new hybrid engines introduced in 2026, his love for the sport has won out.

"First, this is my life," Alonso told BBC Sport in his only English language interview about his decision, which was announced on Tuesday., external

"I have this in my blood and I keep racing and I keep enjoying and this is a way of life, in a way.

"Probably for me the biggest, or the clearest thing to keep racing is I still feel self-confidence that I have something extra.

"And when I think about stepping down or taking a different role in the team or not driving the car or whatever, in a way I feel it should not be like that because I still feel as fast as anybody. So let's have another go."

His own personal performance was only one factor at play in Alonso's decision, he explained in an extensive and open conversation.

Alonso also considered the new rules, and the competitiveness of his team, which has been close to rock bottom for most of this season.

Alonso is regarded as one of the all-time F1 greats, and has created an iconic status over a career that dates back to 2001.

And he continues to reject any suggestion that he has lost any of his ability.

"When I jump in the car, in free practice, I will see some people braking late in a corner, locking up the front tyres here or there, making mistakes there," Alonso says.

"I feel that I'm OK. Or, I'm faster than them.

"So when I get changed and I go back home, even if I'm P18, in a way I feel some satisfaction and pride inside, even if it should not be the case because we are not competitive.

"How will I be in the living room, watching TV, thinking that I can do better? That will be my feeling now. When that changes, if I see that I lost abilities, I lost speed, I lost reflexes, I lost something, then I will be happy to watch from my living room the race.

"At the moment, I feel it was not the time because I'm better than that guy. I'm better than that other guy. I will think like that. And I cannot stop racing if I still think like that."

Alonso has only had a couple of chances this year to prove his point that he's still as good as he ever was. One was at the Dutch Grand Prix, when he finished ninth, holding at bay the faster cars of Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Racing Bulls' Yuki Tsunoda in the final stint.

I suggest to him that it was a typical Alonso drive, proof to those who doubted that he still has it. But he says it will have had no impact on the audience.

"You only prove to people when you are in the podium or you are on TV," he says. "That's where eyes are open, and people remember suddenly that you're still on the grid.

"So now I'm at peace with this period of time that I'm anonymous, and no one knows that we're still there and we're still fast.

"We are preparing ourselves for the moment of truth and that will be a surprise for everybody again."

Along with Max Verstappen and Lando Norris, Alonso has been one of the drivers most critical of the 2026 rules.

Drivers feel the new hybrid engines, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, have diminished F1's challenge.

The key problems are the fact the cars run out of half their energy long before some corners, a process known as "derating", and that some of the sport's most demanding corners have been neutered because they are used to charge the batteries.

Alonso, as is his way, has produced some particularly pithy turns of phrase this season to express his unhappiness.

He has called F1 the "battery world championship". He has described fast corners as "the charging station for the car" and said that "the chef could drive the car" in a particular corner in Bahrain that used to be a major challenge.

And he's been dismissive of the increased number of overtaking moves created by offsets in energy levels between cars, calling them "avoidance actions".

How did he square all that with deciding to keep racing these cars he dislikes so much?

"That's a good question," he says, "because that was the hardest thing for me."

He says he hopes the changes being made to change the power ratio to 60-40 in two steps by 2028 "will make things a little bit easier".

"This year, there have been some good races and some bad races," Alonso says. "Maybe some of the shorter circuits that you had the battery until the braking point are changing the way you perceive the driving.

"And some of the circuits like Silverstone, Spa, Suzuka, they were very bad, you know, because they derate and things like that.

"Maybe even for next year they can tweak a little bit the battery power to have a little bit maybe less battery for longer or something like that because F1 at the moment is not natural driving.

"Reaching the top speed in the middle of the straight, it goes against the driver instinct of braking late and going on power earlier. It seems that if you want to drive these cars fast, you ended up going slower and that's not the way it should be."

Alonso says that, as something of an elder statesman, he "feels some responsibility also in this regard to help the sport" make the right decisions for the future.

And the willingness of governing body the FIA and commercial rights holder F1 to accept there is a problem and make changes to address it has also been a reassurance.

"It does help that the sport keeps chasing ideas and talking to the drivers and the teams (about) how to make things better, even for the next set of regulations," he says.

"This gives me also some hope that I will enjoy more the driving next year than I did this year."

It has been a dismal year for Aston Martin, whose car has been uncompetitive, while Honda's engine has been the worst in the field on the Japanese manufacturer's official return to F1.

But a massive update to the car for the Hungarian Grand Prix cut something like two seconds off lap times, offering hope for next season.

A key influence in Alonso's decision was Adrian Newey, whose arrival as managing technical partner in March 2025 delayed the start of work on this year's car, the first of a cascading series of issues that led to this year's performance.

Alonso has been waiting his entire career to work with the man regarded as the greatest technical mind of his generation, perhaps ever. So giving up after just one, highly compromised, year together felt senseless.

"This team has all the ingredients to have success in the future," Alonso says, "and I didn't feel that this was the moment to leave. It was the moment to keep on going, giving a second chance to Honda as well to fix their problems as well and stay together with the team.

"Adrian was probably the biggest contributor to this. We didn't start it right this year but things are moving in the right direction and he's capable of changing things very quickly.

"Aston is my family. I know Lawrence (Stroll, the owner) and Lance (Stroll, Alonso's team-mate) for many, many years. We keep open conversations, many different topics, every week. And that will be the case also for next year."

Honda's engine upgrade, which debuted at the Dutch Grand Prix at the end of August, was not especially convincing.

Alonso has bad memories of Honda from his time with McLaren from 2015-17, and he admits living through a similar experience again "has been difficult".

But major steps have been taken to address the internal issues at the company and Alonso says: "They are moving in the right direction. There are no guarantees that next year the engine will be completely fixed but all the changes that are happening in Honda made sense, so I have faith.

"The trust that I have in the team, it didn't change even throughout this difficult year. In the future, I don't know how long it's going to take, but it will be a successful team, and I want to be part of it."

There was one final factor - family. Alonso became a father this year when his partner, the Spanish television presenter Melissa Jimenez, gave birth to their son, Leonard, in March.

Has that had any effect on his approach to life and his career?

"I would say not," Alonso says. "I was (initially) thinking yes, and I tried to think about, family first, what will be the best for my son next year if I have this tight calendar or not and things like that.

"But then quickly I realised that it was not really a key factor. This year it was difficult for him to travel; he's only six months old now. But I think next year he will come to 50% of the races or more.

"So I could even enjoy my life more, travelling around the world with my son. That's a huge privilege that I will hopefully enjoy next year.

"Racing next year, it was my natural, final decision. I will be racing in any car, even when I stop Formula 1, but F1 is still in my blood.

"One more year made all the sense in the world for now."

"I see that it would not be only one year, but I don't have any pressure to think about it."

title: Life bright for Gilmour after baseball and World Cup heartache
description: Scotland midfielder Billy Gilmour opens up on the pain of missing out of this summer's World Cup.
fullText:
Billy Gilmour sits at Lesser Hampden, a beaming smile bursting across his face.

The topic of conversation is revolving around him missing the World Cup in the summer, something that could have been defined by harrowing disappointment and regret.

Instead, the Napoli midfielder's face lights up when asked about a night at the baseball in Miami, where the injured Scotland ace was asked to hobble on to the field and hurl the ceremonial first pitch.

"I was nervous," Gilmour tells BBC Scotland, recollecting the evening at the Miami Marlins against the Texas Rangers.

"I was just so happy it wasn't a crap throw, or it was bouncing. It was some experience."

How Manzambi became one of Europe's best young talents

Listen: Can Scotland shock the Swiss at Hampden?

Pocognoli has no concern over Scotland's lack of goals

The maturity and level-headedness of the 25-year-old defies his years.

Just days before he was due to jet off to the United States with the Scotland squad for the first men's World Cup the nation had experienced since before he was born, a crushing blow.

In the farewell game at Hampden against Curacao, he suffered a knee injury that would mean he was left behind. While a body blow to Steve Clarke, his squad and the country, it would have been devastating to a young man with the world stage at his feet.

He admits those initial days were difficult as reality set in, but Gilmour seized the chance to become a supporter across Boston and Miami with his family around him.

"The boys fell on top of me and I've heard something straight away," he said of the injury. "Typical, try to run it off, make sure it was okay.

"It was tough. You have to take yourself away for a couple of days and I did.

"I got to go away for a bit, just kind of switch off and it happened, so I had to deal with it. When you're there around the squad, you try to be as best as you can, as positive as you can.

"When you think of it, how lucky you still are to get to go there and watch the games and be with family and family holiday also."

Gilmour added: "I would be with the team some nights, but the squad and Robbo [captain Andy Robertson] and the gaffer, Steve Clarke, at the time, he basically said: 'Look, if it's too much to come in, don't come in. Stay as much time with the family. Go and experience it with the fans'."

Gilmour was still in Miami when news broke of Clarke's resignation as Scotland head coach. He's a man the Napoli midfielder acknowledges he owes so much to after giving him his debut in 2001.

Now, however, it's the Sebastien Pocognoli era and the former Rangers, Chelsea and Brighton & Hove Albion man seems central to it.

In the 0-0 draw in Slovenia on Saturday, it was Gilmour who caught the attention during a resurgent second half for the Scots.

He is often seen as more of a deep-lying central midfielder, but there was a different dynamic to his game with the absence of club-mate Scott McTominay, who is recovering from a heart procedure.

"When I was younger, I really liked playing higher up, trying to be among it," Gilmour, who is set to feature at Hampden on Tuesday against Switzerland - live on the BBC, said.

"Whenever I get asked to play on the pitch, as long as I'm on the pitch, I'm happy. I just want to play football and enjoy it."

Now 25, there is plenty time to make new memories in a Scotland shirt. Yet, with so many young faces coming into the squad, the Ayrshire man is probably now a senior figure in the group.

It's something he says he embraces, although Gilmour is coy about the prospect of maybe taking on the armband whenever current captain Robertson decides to pass it on.

"For me, it's everyone's dream to be a captain at a club or a country," he said.

"Of course I'd be really proud to, but Robbo's my captain and he's a really good captain as well.

"What he's done for Scotland is incredible and he's very close on the record [most caps held by Kenny Dalglish] and I'm sure he'll get it."

title: Toone and Kelly miss out on Lionesses squad
description: Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone misses out on selection for England's Women's World Cup qualifying matches this month.
fullText:
England manager Sarina Wiegman says Ella Toone and Chloe Kelly have "not been playing to their potential" and that is why they have missed out on selection.

The Lionesses face Greece in their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off matches in October.

Manchester United midfielder Toone, 27, and Arsenal forward Kelly, 28 have had inconsistent starts to the season.

They both had crucial involvements at Euro 2022 and Euro 2025 as the Lionesses won back-to-back titles, but Wiegman is "convinced they can be better".

"Of course, I still believe in these players. They are really good and have shown so much for us," Wiegman told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"But that is also why I didn't pick them this time, because they have not played to their potential in my opinion in the last couple of weeks.

"I had those conversations with them and that was very hard to take. They took it well and of course, they want to work on that."

On reports suggesting Kelly's absence may have been linked to an injury, Wiegman added in her media conference: "I had the conversation with Chloe and for me, it was just what I saw on the pitch. I kept that with football with her."

In addition, Chelsea forward Aggie Beever-Jones and Arsenal duo Lotte Wubben-Moy and Taylor Hinds have not made the 23-player squad.

Captain Leah Williamson returns having missed June's 4-0 defeat by Spain and 3-0 win over Ukraine.

"I think she's played really well in the last few weeks and at the start of the season. She is happy and you can see," added Wiegman.

Could Potter be England's next breakthrough star?

All you need to know about 2027 Women's World Cup

Meanwhile, there is a first senior call-up for Chelsea midfielder Lexi Potter, 20, who has impressed alongside England's Keira Walsh in the Women's Super League.

She has started three of Chelsea's opening four matches and was a standout performer in their 1-0 win over Arsenal on Sunday.

"Her performances were just really good. We started following her closely last season and she got minutes over time," said Wiegman.

"She plays with a lot of courage, a lot of understanding and her decision-making is really good. Her technical ability, we have seen, is really good too.

"What I've seen is that no matter who she plays against, like last Sunday [against Arsenal], it looks like it doesn't bother her at all and she will just play football.

"She played against very high-level players, international players, and she just played. She looked very comfortable. I hope she shows that with us too."

There is also a return to the squad for uncapped midfielder Erica Meg Parkinson, 18, who has excelled since joining North Carolina Courage in the summer.

Manchester City full-back Niamh Charles made her return from injury as a substitute in their 1-0 win over Charlton Athletic on Saturday and is included.

London City Lionesses forward Freya Godfrey and Liverpool defender Grace Fisk are the other two uncapped players named.

England play a double-header against Greece, first in Crete on Friday, 9 October (17:30 BST) and then in Leicester on Tuesday, 13 October (19:30 BST).

If they win the two-legged tie, they progress to round two of the play-offs where they can compete for a place in next summer's Women's World Cup in Brazil.

Defenders: Lucy Bronze (Chelsea), Jess Carter (Gotham FC), Niamh Charles (Manchester City), Grace Fisk (Liverpool), Alex Greenwood (Manchester City), Maya Le Tissier (Manchester United), Esme Morgan (Washington Spirit), Leah Williamson (Arsenal)

Midfielders: Laura Blindkilde Brown (Manchester City), Lucia Kendall (Aston Villa), Erica Meg Parkinson (North Carolina Courage), Lexi Potter (Chelsea), Georgia Stanway (Arsenal), Keira Walsh (Chelsea)

Forwards: Freya Godfrey (London City Lionesses), Lauren Hemp (Manchester City), Lauren James (Chelsea), Beth Mead (Manchester City), Jess Park (Manchester United), Alessia Russo (Arsenal).

title: 'Period of deception' - Pochettino on Man City verdict
description: Former Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino says it is "impossible to turn back time" after Manchester City being found guilty of financial breaches.
fullText:
Former Tottenham and Chelsea manager Mauricio Pochettino says "we have lived through a period of deception" after Manchester City were found guilty of breaking the majority of the charges brought against them by the Premier League.

An independent panel found City to be guilty of a wide range of financial rule breaches, with the Athletic, external reporting on Friday that 114 of the 115 charges against them have been upheld.

Sanctions are yet to be announced, but City plan on appealing against the decision.

The charges relate to a period from 2009-10 to 2017-18, while they were accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations between December 2018 to February 2023.

United States manager Pochettino managed three clubs in the Premier League during that time, with the 54-year-old spending 15 months at Southampton, five years at Tottenham and a single season with Chelsea.

"Whatever punishment [they choose], it's impossible to turn back time," said Pochettino.

"It's done a lot of damage. Many clubs followed the rules and some didn't.

"Maybe they thought that the punishment [wouldn't come for a lot of years] - what are they going to do? An economic punishment? Docking points? It's really hard.

"It is a huge sadness. We get into a situation where what got celebrated wasn't that real, what seemed good maybe wasn't so good, what didn't look good maybe was good but couldn't be good because of what happened.

"We went through something where sporting fairness didn't exist. So, how do you repair everything that was damaged because of that, if it's true all of the 114 rules that were broken, we've lived through a period of deception."

Man City CEO defiant over Premier League charges

Spurs should be awarded 2016-17 title - Pochettino

Man City rule breaches not my concern - Mancini

Earlier this month, Pochettino said Chelsea should be stripped of the 2016-17 Premier League title after being found guilty of historical rule breaches and that it should be "awarded" to his Tottenham side, who finished runners-up.

Sources have told BBC Sport that other top flight clubs are seeking legal advice over possible compensation claims following the decision against City.

City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation.

The club were referred to an independent commission. A behind-closed-doors hearing began in September 2024 and ran for about 12 weeks.

"Where were the controls?" said Pochettino on City being found guilty. "That's what gets my attention. Where were the controls?

"If I remember being at Southampton, then Tottenham - I remember building [the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium] and not having the economic possibility of a transfer for 18 months.

"I think we were the only team in the history of the Premier League with 18 months without [making a transfer].

"Tottenham was fighting for titles with those above us and every year in the top four, getting to the semi-finals of the Champions League without being able to do a transfer for 18 months, all because we needed to get used to the [Premier League financial controls]?

"They were so strict with us but also so lenient with others. Because of that, that's why I say: it's all very strange."
