title: Gordon Johncock, a two-time winner of the Indianapolis 500, has died at 90
description: Gordon Johncock, a two-time Indianapolis 500 champion and winner of 25 career IndyCar races, has died.  Johncock died from natural causes Monday at his home in South Branch, Michigan, a spokesman for the family told The Associated Press.  Johncock competed in one of IndyCar's golden eras.
fullText:
INDIANAPOLIS (AP) — Gordon Johncock, a two-time Indianapolis 500 champion and winner of 25 career IndyCar races, has died. He was 90.

Johncock died from natural causes Monday at his home in South Branch, Michigan, a spokesman for the family told The Associated Press.

Johncock competed in one of IndyCar's golden eras. He raced annually at The Brickyard against the likes of four-time winners A.J. Foyt, Rick Mears and Al Unser, three-time winners Bobby Unser and Johnny Rutherford and 1969 race winner Mario Andretti, among others.

And yet, with so many big personalities in the series then, Johncock managed to carve out his own niche with his smalltown roots and penchant for wearing flannel shirts and jeans. He won the 1976 USAC title in an IndyCar.

But he was best known for his Indy 500 wins. His first came in 1973, one of the race's most tragic months. His second came in 1982 when he outdueled Mears to the finish line for what was then the closest winning margin in race history at 0.16 seconds. It's still the seventh-closest.

"By far the biggest thrill of my racing career was winning Indianapolis in 1982," Johncock once said. "The way it happened, the competition, so many near wins after 1973 and it all came together and the car lasted in 1982. Plus, I've got amazing respect for Rick Mears — one of the very best. He was never my teammate, but I think we could have been good ones."

The month of May in 1973 was marred by rain, which forced the race to be run over three days and shortened to 133 of 200 laps; two horrific crashes that resulted in the deaths of drivers Art Pollard and Swede Savage, Johncock's teammate with Patrick Racing who was severely injured in the race. Savage was pronounced dead in early July.

A pit crew member for Patrick Racing also died after being hit by a fire truck responding to Savage's crash, And driver David "Salt" Walther suffered severe burns when his car burst into flames as it hit the catch fence in the front straightaway as the race began, injuring nearly a dozen fans.

Yet Johncock, who started 11th, overcame the chaos and was one of just two cars on the lead lap when more rain forced the race to be stopped.

"I didn't feel that race was given to us," Johncock once told Autoweek. "If we had only led one or two laps and happened to be settin' there when they stopped it and won it that way, then I guess you wouldn't have earned it very well."

Johncock started driving the family's John Deere tractor in Hastings, Michigan, when he was 5 years old. He joined the IndyCar Series in 1964 and finished fifth in the 500 as a rookie in 1965. Johncock wound up competing in the 500 24 times, tied for fifth-most. He made three starts on the front row, nine times on the second row and completed 7,895 miles while leading a total of 339 laps. He finished third in the 500 in 1976 and 1978, and had two fourth place finishes.

From 1964-92, Johncock made 262 career IndyCar starts and retired twice.

In 1967, joining A.J. Foyt as the sport's only owner/driver, and he was one of the last living drivers to have competed in both the front and rear-engine IndyCar eras. And like drivers from that generation, he also competed in NASCAR — making 21 starts, including three at the Daytona 500 where he finished fifth in 1973.

Johncock was inducted into the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Hall of Fame in 1997 and the International Motorsports Hall of Fame in 1999.

Away from the track, Johncock loved farming and the forestry business — which explained his clothing choice and why people referred to his fashion choices as "Johncock casual."

He is survived by his wife, Sue; three daughters, two sons, two stepdaughters, 12 grandchildren, 17 great-grandchildren and one great-great grandchild.

title: 7 of Matthew Mayich’s teammates ask ASU to put hockey coach Greg Powers on leave
description: PHOENIX – Seven Arizona State men’s hockey players asked ASU President Michael Crow on Monday to place the Sun Devils coaching staff on administrative leave. They say the university’s review...
fullText:
PHOENIX – Seven Arizona State men's hockey players asked ASU President Michael Crow on Monday to place the Sun Devils coaching staff on administrative leave. They say the university's review of the Aug. 20 workout that left teammate Matthew Mayich on life support got key facts wrong and did not hold anyone responsible.

In their 26-page letter, sent through their attorney, Tim Casey, the players say Mayich never received water during a workout that ran more than 75 minutes. They also say he showed signs of distress long before he collapsed and was not properly cooled before paramedics arrived.

The ASU players sent the letter anonymously, writing that they fear retaliation from coach Greg Powers and his assistants, who "decide our playing time, scholarship levels, and roster status."

The news prompted Arizona's House and Senate education chairs to ask the Arizona Board of Regents Monday to retain an independent investigator to examine the incident.

The seven players who sent the letter make up roughly a quarter of the roster. They wrote that other teammates share their concerns but did not sign for the same reason. The letter says Casey holds "signed attestations" from the players confirming they are members of the team and were in attendance when Mayich suffered heatstroke.

"We should not have to choose between telling the truth about August 20 and keeping what we have worked our whole lives for," they wrote.

Along with leave for the staff who approved, ran and supervised the workout, the players also requested:

An investigation by "an agency outside the university"

Written assurance that no player will be punished for speaking out

An interim coaching staff during the investigation, naming former Coyotes captain Shane Doan as "an excellent candidate"

Mayich is a 21-year-old sophomore transfer from Stoney Creek, Ontario, in Canada. He had been in Arizona eight days when he collapsed at the end of the team's first preseason workout at Sun Angel Stadium. Family attorney Robert Carey has said Mayich suffered an exertional heatstroke that deprived his brain of oxygen and has no chance of a meaningful recovery.

2026-09-28 Hockey Team Members' Letter to ASU President Michael M. CrowDownload

The Sept. 28 letter responds point-by-point to the initial review by ASU Senior Vice President James Rund, delivered to Crow on Sept. 21.

The workout was run by Tim Ziesel, a former Green Beret whom an ASU booster introduced to the program.

ASU policy bars outside consultants from working with athletes until they are approved. Rund's report shows a request to use Ziesel was submitted Aug. 12 without a training plan, but the report does not say whether the request was ever reviewed or approved.

The players wrote that the only water break came 35 to 45 minutes in, not at 20 minutes as Rund's report found. When Powers told Ziesel to get the players water, Ziesel said, "Oh yeah, I forgot, you guys need water," according to the letter. Only the first eight or so players to finish a bear crawl reached the bottles, the letter said, adding that Mayich was still crawling and never received any water.

Rund's report said Mayich appeared to struggle during the final drill, a medicine-ball relay. The players wrote that he was disoriented much earlier and could not carry a teammate during a buddy-carry exercise. At one point, they wrote, he had to lean on a teammate to stay upright.

Ziesel left after assigning the medicine-ball relay, though Mayich was struggling before he left, according to the players. Only ASU coaches and an athletic trainer were supervising when Mayich collapsed.

"No one at ASU properly monitored him during the workout and no one intervened," the players wrote.

The players said the trainer sat Mayich upright twice, contradicting the report's statement that he was kept on the ground. The letter said Mayich lay in direct sun for several minutes. Cooling came from a few towels, squirt bottles and less than a minute of warm water from a garden hose, the letter said, despite ASU's heat policy calling for a cold-water immersion tub..

There was no tub on site, and no one used the tub inside Mullett Arena.

The players also dispute the report's statements that Mayich was acclimatized. They wrote that his only previous outdoor work was a few five-minute stretches broken up by breaks in air conditioning. They also cited a video of one drill showing the players in a "plank" position in direct sunlight, which contradicts the report's description of a mostly cloudy sky.

After an ambulance arrived and took Mayich to the hospital, the letter states, Powers told players he had "just a little heat stroke" and "just needs an IV." The next day, the players stated, the coach told them Mayich would be fine and the team went ahead with practice.

ASU opens its season at 5 p.m. Friday at Lindenwood. The letter asks Crow to act "if the facts in this report warrant it" and to name an interim coaching staff before the opener.

Meanwhile, House Education Committee Chairman Matt Gress, R-Phoenix, and Senate Education Committee Chairman Hildy Angius, R-Bullhead City, cite unresolved questions about whether ASU followed its own policies.

"Seven players who were on that field have raised serious questions that ASU's own review does not answer," Gress said in a statement. "We need an independent investigation to determine whether ASU followed its own rules, who was responsible for protecting these athletes, and what happened when Matthew Mayich showed signs of distress. ASU should not be left to investigate its own conduct and decide whether anyone should be held accountable."

title: Luka Doncic: Walker Kessler will be an 'amazing fit' for Lakers
description: At the Lakers' Media Day on Monday, Luka Doncic expressed optimism and excitement about playing with center Walker Kessler.
fullText:
The Los Angeles Lakers held Media Day in advance of training camp on Monday at UCLA Health Training Center in El Segundo. The mood was positive and upbeat, as many of the team's players seemed excited and were looking forward to the new season.

The team has nine new players, and of them, center Walker Kessler is expected to have the biggest impact. Los Angeles gave up two future first-round draft picks and two pick swaps to get Kessler while signing the shot-blocking master to a four-year, $130 million contract. Some feel the franchise gave up too much to get him, but others are positive he will live up to his price tag.

One reason the Lakers invested so much in Kessler is that Luka Doncic wanted them to get a prominent center this summer. On Monday, Doncic said Kessler will be an "amazing fit" for the Lakers and greatly help the team, and he admitted that going up against Kessler in the past was difficult, per Khobi Price of the California Post.

Luka Doncic, when asked about why/how he identified Walker Kessler as a player he wanted on the Lakers, says Walker was always tough to play against. Added that Walker will be an "amazing fit for us" and "he’s going to help us a lot.”

Kessler isn't just a great shot-blocker -- he's also a fantastic rebounder and lob threat. Plus, at age 25, he still has some upward potential on the offensive end, especially after experimenting with some 3-point shooting early last season before he was shut down for the year due to a torn labrum.

He said on Monday that his surgically repaired shoulder is fully healthy and feeling even better than it was before he sustained his injury.

Walker Kessler says he is 110% healthy and his surgically repaired shoulder is feeling better than it ever has before.

Kessler has career averages of 9.5 points, 9.3 rebounds and 2.4 blocks in 25.3 minutes a game through four seasons. He previously played on a Utah Jazz team that was allegedly tanking, but he's now on a Lakers team that expects to make the playoffs.

title: How FIBA 3x3 Basketball Went From A Business Case To An Olympic Sport
description: FIBA 3x3 basketball evolved from a Youth Olympic experiment into a global sport, driven by gender equity, digital engagement and a spectator-first approach ahead of LA28.
fullText:
(This is part one of a two-part story based on a Forbes exclusive interview with Alex Sanchez on September 22, 2026. All quotes are taken directly from a transcript of the interview.)

In 2010, Alex Sanchez was not trying to save basketball, reinvent basketball or even necessarily build a new Olympic sport. He was doing something much more familiar to the world of business. He was analyzing an investment opportunity.

At the time, FIBA 3x3 basketball was being played at the Youth Olympic Games, but the International Basketball Federation wanted to know whether the abbreviated version of basketball was something more than a novelty. Could three-on-three basketball become a legitimate sport with its own athletes, competitions, commercial potential and global audience? Sanchez, who had an MBA from the University of Chicago and a background in private equity, venture capital and consulting, was asked to find out.

Sixteen years later, that analysis looks remarkably prescient.

Three-on-three basketball is now an Olympic sport, and it will arrive in Los Angeles for the 2028 Olympic Games with FIBA Managing Director Alex Sanchez still helping guide its global development.

"I did the analysis," Sanchez recalled in an interview with Forbes. "At the end of it … my conclusion at the time was that there was a real business case to develop 3x3 as a standalone discipline."

But there was an even bigger possibility. Sanchez concluded that 3x3 could become an Olympic sport if FIBA did the right things.

Sanchez's path to FIBA was not the conventional route for a basketball executive. Born in Barcelona to a Spanish father and German mother, Sanchez attended a German school in Spain and developed what he describes as two cultural perspectives on the same things. Before joining FIBA, he had already lived and worked in several European countries, including Spain, Belgium, Germany and the United Kingdom. He eventually came to the United States to earn an MBA at the University of Chicago, attracted in part by the finance-driven approach of the university's business program. After graduate school came private equity, venture capital and consulting.

The organization's previous secretary general wanted an objective analysis of 3x3. The sport was appearing at the Youth Olympic Games, but FIBA wanted to know whether there was a sustainable business proposition underneath it. Sanchez deliberately approached the assignment without treating it as a basketball project.

"I analyzed it as it would be a new brand for shoes or a new engine for planes," he said.

That distinction mattered. Instead of asking whether basketball fans liked three-on-three basketball, Sanchez was essentially asking whether a new sporting property could create a sufficiently differentiated product, audience and business model. The answer was yes. The next question was much harder: What would FIBA have to build to give 3x3 a legitimate opportunity to become Olympic? Sanchez and his colleagues produced a concept paper laying out what would have to happen.

That roadmap would require much more than changing the number of players on the court.

One of the first strategic decisions was gender equity. From the beginning, FIBA wanted men's and women's 3x3 to develop together. Sanchez said the organization was determined that national-team competitions would include men and women at the same time so the women's side would have an opportunity to grow at a comparable pace. The strategy was straightforward: If women's 3x3 were treated as an afterthought, it could fall behind.

Instead, gender equity became part of the architecture of the sport.

The second major milestone was professional competition. FIBA needed to demonstrate that 3x3 was not simply something athletes played occasionally at a Youth Olympic event. It needed professional athletes competing year-round. That led to the launch of the FIBA 3x3 World Tour in 2012, less than two years after FIBA's board decided to pursue the discipline. For Sanchez, this was critical.

"It had to have its own professional competition league tour," he explained.

The World Tour provided something that a collection of exhibition events could not: evidence that 3x3 could support a professional sporting ecosystem. It showed that athletes could make 3x3 their sport rather than treating it as a side activity.

And it gave FIBA an increasingly visible international product.

The next challenge was perhaps the most fundamental: What exactly should 3x3 basketball be?

FIBA could simply have taken traditional basketball, removed two players from each side and played the game on a half court. Instead, Sanchez said FIBA deliberately adapted the rules. The goal was to bring the organized version of the game closer to the way people actually played street basketball. That philosophy eventually became central to the sport's identity.

"The idea was to put the spectator in the center of all our changes or all our decisions," Sanchez said.

The objective was not simply to preserve basketball's traditional form. It was to create an experience. FIBA eventually described 3x3 with a simple phrase: "most thrilling urban sport." That phrase captured the strategy. The venues mattered. The rules mattered. The pace mattered. The presentation mattered.

And even the equipment became part of the product.

FIBA developed a ball specifically for 3x3. It is smaller than a traditional men's basketball but heavier, a combination Sanchez said was designed around the characteristics of the game and particularly outdoor grip and shooting. That might sound like a small detail.

The creation of a dedicated 3x3 ball was another indication that FIBA was no longer treating the discipline as simply a modified version of five-on-five basketball. It was becoming its own sporting product.

Perhaps the most interesting part of Sanchez's 3x3 strategy is that the sport was being designed for spectators before smartphones became the dominant way many younger fans consume sports. Today, that approach looks almost obvious.

A 3x3 game takes place on a half court with six players on the floor. The action is compact. The games are short. And the format naturally produces frequent highlights. Sanchez believes those characteristics make 3x3 particularly well suited for mobile viewing.

"You actually can see them everywhere," he said, referring to the short games and abundance of highlights.

That became an important part of FIBA's digital strategy. The organization created a social-media operation specifically focused on producing clips, polls and other digital content for platforms including Facebook, Twitter, Instagram and TikTok. The target audience was especially important. Sanchez said the core social audience falls largely within the 13-to-35 age range.

The sport therefore wasn't simply being played for the audience sitting courtside. It was also being packaged to be consumed by the person watching on a phone.

According to Sanchez, FIBA 3x3 now has more than 10 million social-media followers. Its dedicated social-media channels generate well above 1 billion views annually, according to Sanchez, approaching 2 billion views. Those figures are part of the story of how an experimental discipline became a global sporting property. But Sanchez believes another characteristic is just as important.

The audience is geographically distributed.

Rather than being concentrated primarily in one continent, Sanchez said 3x3 has developed meaningful participation and interest across Europe, the Americas and Asia. That distribution is rooted in something deceptively simple. A basketball hoop and a basketball are enough to begin.

As Sanchez put it, "if you have a ball and you have a hoop, actually, basically everybody will end up" trying to play.

That accessibility may be one of 3x3's greatest advantages.

For many basketball players, three-on-three is not something they learned from a federation. It is something they discovered after school at a park, in a driveway, or on an outdoor court with friends. The rules may vary. The competition may be informal. The stakes may be nothing more than bragging rights. But the fundamental experience is remarkably universal.

The beauty of the game was its simplicity. You didn't need a full roster, a coach or an elaborate facility. You needed a ball, a basket and somebody willing to play.

FIBA has taken that intuitive experience and built a professional sport around it without destroying the essence of the game.

This article was originally published on Forbes.com

title: US Senate passes landmark overhaul of college sports
description: The US Senate approved a landmark federal framework for college sports Monday, voting 72-22 to bring order to a multibillion-dollar industry whose biggest events can draw television audiences comparable to major professional championships.More than 30 million people watched January's college football national championship on TV while the major conferences -- regional groupings of universities that organize competition and negotiate media rights -- have signed multibillion-dollar broadcasting con
fullText:
The US Senate approved a landmark federal framework for college sports Monday, voting 72-22 to bring order to a multibillion-dollar industry whose biggest events can draw television audiences comparable to major professional championships.

The bipartisan Protect College Sports Act would regulate how universities pay athletes, restrict transfers and give the governing NCAA limited protection from antitrust lawsuits after years of court battles transformed the economics of college athletics.

The vote was one of the Senate's last major legislative acts before lawmakers leave Washington to campaign for the November 3 midterm elections.

The bill now goes to the House of Representatives, which is already in recess until after Election Day, leaving a narrow window for Congress to complete work before a new legislature takes office in January.

President Donald Trump's administration has endorsed the legislation, and the 80-year-old leader himself cheered the bill's passage Monday night, posting to his Truth Social platform that "it will not only save college sports, it will save the colleges themselves."

Unlike university sports in most countries, American college athletics is a vast commercial enterprise.

More than 30 million people watched January's college football national championship on TV while the major conferences -- regional groupings of universities that organize competition and negotiate media rights -- have signed multibillion-dollar broadcasting contracts.

The legislation follows years of upheaval during which athletes won the right to profit from their names and images and, following a 2025 court settlement, universities began paying players directly.

It would establish national rules governing those payments and allow schools to spend nearly $50 million annually through revenue-sharing and other funds.

Athletes would generally be allowed one transfer without sitting out a season, while agents' fees would be capped at five percent.

The bill also provides longer-term scholarship and healthcare protections and seeks to safeguard women's and Olympic sports.

Supporters argue that nationwide rules are needed to replace a patchwork of state laws and repeated litigation.

"Student athletes deserve to get paid. They deserve real protections. And high school athletes deserve a fair shot to compete," said Senator Ted Cruz, who co-sponsored the bill.

"The Protect College Sports Act delivers that while protecting women's and Olympic sports and preserving the game we love for generations to come," the Texas Republican added.

But the measure has divided Democrats and drawn opposition from racial equality activists, labor unions and the Congressional Black Caucus.

Critics say its antitrust protections give too much power back to the NCAA while limiting athletes' legal rights and leaving unresolved whether college players should ultimately be treated as employees entitled to collective bargaining.

The House could seek changes, potentially forcing another Senate vote and complicating efforts to send the legislation to Trump before the current Congress expires.

76ers news: LeBron James drops Media Day mic about bailing on family for Philly appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

At Media Day, ahead of his 24th NBA season, LeBron James' excited about his Philadephia 76ers debut. In pursuit of his fifth championship, James has loft goals for the 76ers, but understands it will take time for his new team to blossom into title contenders. He's looking forward to the process.

James has led every single team he's played for to a title, and knows the work that lies ahead for the 2026-27 76ers, he said, per The Philly Voice's Adam Aaronson.

"Work needs to be done, and I'm ready to put the work in," James said.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

LeBron concluded his press conference at Sixers Media Day by stating he didn't move away from his family to lose in the second round of the playoffs, thus reminding 76ers fans of winning a title being the ultimate goal.

76ers veteran LeBron James knows what it takes for a team to win a championship. It's one thing he undoubtely has in common with 76ers head coach Nick Nurse, who guided the Raptors to a title in 2019.

One thing James and Nurse both agreed upon is the importance of being an elite defensive team, James revealed, per Mind The Game podcast.

"I've been able to be on some really good defensive teams in my career, and defense always comes down to the first thing: pride. It's a pride thing," James said. "I'm not going to allow my guy to continue to exploit me or beat me or whatever the case may be. There has to be some pride."

For James, rattling opposing teams' offense is critical for the 76ers' success this upcoming season.

"At the end of the day, the best defense never stops the best offense anyways, and that's okay," James added. "But if we can make teams uncomfortable, if we can make teams turn the ball over, if we can make teams just not be in a rhythm like they're accustomed to being in a rhythm versus other teams, it gives us another opportunity. It gives us more possessions. We want to try to win the possession game."

LeBron and the 76ers will begin their preseason schedule with a matchup against the Knicks on October 5.

title: Gordon Johncock, two-time Indy 500 winner, dies at 90
description: Gordon Johncock, a two-time Indianapolis 500 winner and Motorsports Hall of Famer, died Monday, Sept. 28 at the age of 90, his family announced.
fullText:
Gordon Johncock, a two-time Indianapolis 500 champion, died Monday, Sept. 28 in his South Branch, Michigan, home. He was 90 years old.

Johncock won the Indy 500 in 1973 and 1982. He is survived by his wife, Sue, five children – Peggy, Patsy, Pamilee, Wally and Gordon Jr. – stepdaughter (Valerie Heffelbowe), 12 grandchildren, 17 great grandchildren and one great great grandchild.

Johncock was not one to be in the light often. After his second retirement from racing, he owned Quigley Lumber, a Michigan business where he cut and sold timber.

"I've never been a person who wanted to be out in public and make appearances – I don't like that stuff," Johncock told IndyStar in 2016. "I've never said this before, but that's one reason I never pressured Roger Penske for a ride. He had his guys doing PR work constantly; there never was any relief.

"Although, if I had (joined Team Penske), I probably would have had a lot better record than I did."

Johncock was inducted into the IMS Museum Hall of Fame in 1997 and the Motorsports Hall of Fame of America in 2002. He won 25 races, 20 poles and the 1976 IndyCar (then USAC) championship. Johncock competed in 24 Indy 500s, finishing in the top five eight times and leading 339 laps. Johncock also started 21 races in the NASCAR Cup Series, although he was never a full-time driver.

Johncock said the 1982 Indy 500, which he won by just 0.160 seconds over Rick Mears, was the "biggest thrill" of his racing career. Johncock outdueled Mears, who has a record-tying four Indy 500 wins, by the sixth slimmest margin in Indy 500 history (at the time it was the closest margin). Johncock felt more gratitude for his second Indy 500 win after his first came in a rain-shortened, 133-lap race.

"The way it happened, the competition, so many near wins after 1973 and it all came together and the car lasted in 1982," Johncock said in 2023. "Plus I've got amazing respect for Rick Mears – one of the very best. He was never my teammate but I think we could have been good ones. I think the more pressure that was on me during a race the better I did and with the car pushing so bad and Rick on my tail, it was great. I'll never forget it. There are so many memories from that day – the crazy start, my final pit stop and winning by such a narrow margin – lastly pushing so hard the final laps with Rick in my mirrors."

Johncock was part of one of the most accomplished rookie classes in Indy 500 history in 1965. That was the same year that Mario Andretti and Al Unser debuted in the Greatest Spectacle in Racing. In Johncock's final Indy 500 start in 1992, he became the second oldest driver to compete in the race at 55 years and 272 days old. Only A.J. Foyt, who was 57 years and 129 days old in that same 1992 race, has done it at an older age than Johncock.

Johncock drove for most of his career at Patrick Racing, where he won both of his Indy 500s. He made 76 podiums in his career.

Zion Brown is IndyStar's motorsports reporter. Follow him at @z10nbr0wn. Get IndyStar's motor sports coverage sent directly to your inbox with our Motor Sports newsletter.

fullText:
The Miami Dolphins are 0-3 and have lost all three of their games by at least two touchdowns this season. It's a little early to start talking about whether they could go winless this season, but it's never too early to start thinking about Miami Heat basketball as Dolphins' head coach Jeff Hafley learned on Monday.

Hafley was surprised by the lack of turnout to his regular Monday press conference following a 24-10 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. When Hafley asked if this was everyone a member of the press who must have drawn the short straw in the newsroom told him that it was Heat media day.

Dolphins HC Jeff Hafley was visibly taken aback by the lack of reporters at his press conference today, with many of them attending Heat Media Day instead:

Coach: "is this everyone that's coming …?"

Reporter: "it's Heat media day."

It's clear what team runs this city 🔥 pic.twitter.com/rPlngtUW5Q

— HeatMuse (@Heat_Muse) September 28, 2026

Today was the first opportunity for many media members to talk to Giannis Antetokounmpo. People needed to know about the iguana situation. Questions about a gameplan for the undefeated Minnesota Vikings could wait.

At Heat Media Day, Giannis talks about his recent run-in with an iguana at his home 😂 pic.twitter.com/0tfiQzuYZC

The good news for Hafley is that the media should return next week.

Not to mention there aren't any conflicts with the Heat and Dolphins' schedules again the rest of the year. title: Clippers news: LA sends strong message to fans at Media Day after Kawhi Leonard scandal
description: LOS ANGELES — The LA Clippers officially kicked off their season on Monday with Media Day at Intuit Dome. It was the first step in what will be a long journey back after the NBA handed down one of the harshest punishments in sports for their role in the Kawhi Leonard salary cap circumvention scandal. In addition to the loss of five future first […] The post Clippers news: LA sends strong message to fans at Media Day after Kawhi Leonard scandal appeared first on ClutchPoints.
fullText:
Clippers news: LA sends strong message to fans at Media Day after Kawhi Leonard scandal appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

LOS ANGELES — The LA Clippers officially kicked off their season on Monday with Media Day at Intuit Dome. It was the first step in what will be a long journey back after the NBA handed down one of the harshest punishments in sports for their role in the Kawhi Leonard salary cap circumvention scandal.

In addition to the loss of five future first round draft picks, the NBA's punishment included a one year suspension for owner Steve Ballmer and a six month suspension for President of Basketball Operations Lawrence Frank.

That means general manager Trent Redden has been promoted to interim President and Mark Hughes is promoted to interim general manager.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Before Media Day officially kicked off with player interviews, Redden and Clippers head coach Tyronn Lue met with members of the media and provided a lengthy opening statement with regards to the NBA's investigation.

"Obviously, this took a little longer than we had hoped. You guys deserved to hear from us before this. Our fans deserved to hear from us before this. And for that, we're sorry. We've been listening, though, not just being quiet, but listening to the thoughts, the concerns, and feeling the emotions of our fan base. They mean everything to us. Their pain through this time is real. And we feel it and we hear them, as well as our staff members who are proud to be part of this organization. We hope to fulfill our promises to them to build their trust and move forward through this time.

"The penalties we are facing are significant and we will comply with it. It will go hand in hand with our mandate to our fans, to work to build their confidence as we go through the NBA's mandates and penalties this season. Personally, Ty and I are going to miss [Lawrence Frank] and Steve [Ballmer] immensely. We wouldn't be here if it weren't for them. And they have led us through a lot of different times. It will be a challenge without them, but what they prepared us for, although this unique circumstance is new. But the opportunities they've given us, the knowledge they've taught us will lead us, and they put together a staff that can offer us behind us and help fulfill all the things that we want to this season.

"In addition, Ty and I have both been able to meet with John Gibson, our interim governor, who is a leader and a steward for us during this difficult time, not just to us in basketball operations, but also on the business side. These challenges are large, not just the penalties, but some of the injuries that we've already faced as well. This franchise often has done its best work with his back against the wall. Training camp starts tomorrow. And we've got a deep group of players that have shown competitive spirit time and again, in a coaching staff led by Ty, who we thinks the best in the NBA. We hope to represent our fans the same way we always had in dark times by coming out and fighting."

Trent Redden opens up Clippers media day with a statement apologizing to fans and saying they’re listening to everything that’s been said about them. pic.twitter.com/QXc82eZdEN

— Tomer Azarly (@TomerAzarly) September 28, 2026

The statement is primarily directed towards the fans, who have been mostly neglected throughout this entire summer after the NBA came out and handed the Clippers their punishment for circumventing the salary cap with Kawhi Leonard.

Coach Tyronn Lue also added his statement on the morale of the LA Clippers franchise

"It's been difficult," Lue said. "Losing Steve and L. for this time, but I give our players a lot of credit. Since Day 1, we said we wanted everyone back the day after Labor Day, and we've had guys in the gym for two months now. Just working and trying to get better. I give our players a lot of credit for being here every single day. Everybody showed up. The leadership is great, the morale is great, even in these tough situations. That's good to see when you have your players coming in and giving everything that they have. A lot of teams don't have that."

The LA Clippers have traveled to Hawaii for training camp, where they'll be until they take on the Golden State Warriors on Sunday, October 4th.

title: Rams could be without starting cornerback, tight end vs. Eagles
description: Jaylen Watson and Terrance Ferguson are likely to miss Sunday’s game against the Eagles, while the Rams remain hopeful Puka Nacua can return
fullText:
The Rams' trip to Philadelphia is still several days away, but their injury concerns are already taking shape on both sides of the ball.

Los Angeles coach Sean McVay said Monday that cornerback Jaylen Watson dislocated his shoulder during Sunday's game against Denver and "probably" will miss Week 4 against the Eagles, according to Rams reporter Stu Jackson. McVay said the team has not discussed placing Watson on injured reserve. He has dealt with the injury before, ESPN's Sarah Barshop said.

Sean McVay said CB Jaylen Watson dislocated his shoulder. McVay said Watson "probably" will miss this week's game against Eagles, but he won't go on Injured Reserve. IR isn't something they've discussed.

Sean McVay said he imagines TE Terrance Ferguson will miss the Rams' Week 4 game against the Eagles with his ankle injury.

Terrance Ferguson also is likely to miss Sunday's game after suffering a medial ankle sprain. McVay described fellow tight end Colby Parkinson, who sustained an AC joint sprain in his shoulder, as more day-to-day. Those injuries could thin a group the Rams have used extensively in their passing game. Ferguson caught six passes for 54 yards and a touchdown against the Giants in Week 2. The Rams' participation reports later this week will better indicate who can play in Philadelphia.

The outlook is more encouraging for wide receiver Puka Nacua. McVay said he is "hopeful" Nacua will play against the Eagles after missing the Rams' past two games with a hip injury. Los Angeles had listed him as doubtful for Sunday's game in Denver. Watson's likely absence would affect the Rams' defense against Jalen Hurts and Philadelphia's receivers. Nacua's potential return could restore one of Matthew Stafford's top targets. Neither player has received a Week 4 game designation yet; those decisions will come after the teams practice this week.

title: Here's who won the games on Monday's rain-shortened schedule in RI
description: Volleyball, soccer and field hockey scores from Sept. 28 and Tuesday's full schedule of games
fullText:
EAST PROVIDENCE – Exactly how Providence Country Day or Bay View might match up against Cranston East will remain a mystery, but at least one question was answered Monday afternoon.

It will take a playoff meeting for anything to separate the Division III Knights and Bengals girls soccer squads. Injury Fund action couldn't do it, and this draw in the rain on the Providence Country Day campus also wasn't enough.

The elements would have been tricky enough to negotiate on the back end of this days-long storm. Add in a turf surface that played like lightning once it was wet and the conditions were too difficult for attackers to manage too many sharp chances. Providence Country Day keeper Iris Morkunas and Bay View keeper Taylor Pitney each kept a clean sheet while navigating a couple tense moments at each end.

The Knights (6-0-2) entered as winners of five straight and fresh off 36 goals in that span. The Bengals (5-1-1) held on at times but did enough to keep their city rivals away from goal. Giada Palano's sliding challenge late in the first half forced a deflected shot to loop over the crossbar and Pitney leaped just in time to stop a shot from distance in the second half that nearly bounced over her head and in.

Morkunas did her best work in the second half, particularly inside the final 10 minutes. Bay View earned a corner kick with the clock winding down and the ball was eventually played out to Kenzie Mooney about 30 yards from the left post. She cracked a right-footed drive that reached the cage on the fly, but Morkunas positioned herself perfectly to make a catch as the whistle sounded.

The two sides played to a 1-1 draw in late August and have since cruised through the regular season to date. The Bengals opened with a Division II loss against Burrillville but are unbeaten in six matches against their own table. Providence Country Day used a lone goal to beat Juanita Sanchez, 1-0, and was held to a scoreless draw by Davies before its recent sizzling streak.

The Thunderbolts entered the day a perfect 7-0-0 and don't have either Bay View or the Knights on their schedule during the regular season. They could avoid both sides all the way to the title match at Rhode Island College – this currently would be a meeting of No. 2 and No. 3 seeds in the bracket. Pawtucket, Johnston, Davies, Blackstone Valley Prep and West Warwick came into the week rounding out the top eight in the standings.

Eiley Simmons bagged the eventual winner and the Chargers added two goals just seconds apart to beat the Quakers, 3-0, in Division I.

Dylan Whitman set up the opener in the 53rd minute, dropping a pass for Simmons to force a deflected shot past the keeper. It stayed 1-0 until the 66th minute when Claire Short hit the top right corner to double the advantage. Maura Stelik put away a Morgan Brucker rebound just moments later as Chariho iced the result.

Savana Debont-Fitzgerald was forced to make just one save to earn the shutout, as the defense in front of her was strong from the Chargers (5-3-1). Marielle Nassiff made 10 saves for Moses Brown (1-5-0).

Maeve Soden continued her strong start to the season as the Avengers eased past the Falcons, 5-1, in Division I.

Soden triggered the attack with two goals and an assist, as East Greenwich built a 3-0 halftime cushion and never looked back. Claudia Hollingsworth, Maeve Monaghan and Izzy MacMillan each added a goal, Elizabeth Low dished out two assists and Vivien Marano chipped in another helper for the Avengers (5-2-0).

Abigail Frias netted a late goal in the second half for Cranston West (0-8-0). Alexa Ramirez finished with five saves.

North Smithfield 3, Classical 0

East Greenwich 5, Cranston West 1

Cumberland 0, East Providence 0

Hendricken 2, South Kingstown 0

North Kingstown 1, Portsmouth 0

The Rebels rallied from an early deficit and edged the Lions in overtime in this Division I matchup. Lincoln struck first in the second quarter when Laura Bello finished a play set up by Molly Comtois with 9:40 remaining for a 1-0 lead.

South Kingstown answered in the third quarter as Lyndee Conley scored off an assist from Marah Nelson with 1:27 left in the frame to even the score. SK completed the comeback in overtime when Reva Patel netted the game-winner with 9:21 remaining, converting a feed from ChloeRoebuck.

Harper Rodman made seven saves for South Kingstown, while EmmalynAraujo stopped three shots for Lincoln. Both teams finished with four shots on goal.

Lincoln School's Arianna Casey scored twice - the first at 10:49 of the fourth quarter which tied the game at 2-2 and second sent the game into overtime, and the second tally which came with only seven seconds left to go in the extra frame to lift the Lynx to victory over the Clippers. Sophie Green-Sermak had the other goal for LS and goalie Lucy Camara recorded 12 saves in the win

Nora Pepin and Tessa Nicastro both scored for Cumberland and goalie Emma Maccio collected for saves.

Solid performances by Amaya Womack (17 kills and 1 ace), Marlowe Castile (6 kills and 6 aces) and Dara Agramonte (4 kills, 20 assists, 5 digs) helped the Purple sweep the Chargers, 25-12, 25-20, 25-17.

For Chariho, Emma McGovern recorded 6 kills, Nicole Raymond had 9 digs and Abby Tiernan dished off 10 assists in the loss.

Riley Fogarty led the Eagles' attack with 14 kills and added five digs, while Charlotte Farrell contributed eight kills and two blocks. Melissa Freshman directed the offense with 22 assists and chipped in nine digs as Barrington controlled play throughout the straight-set victory, 25-21, 25-16, 25-22.

For the Falcons, Emily Nodzis paced the defense with 17 digs in the loss.

The Patriots rode two nip-and-tuck sets into a sweep at home.

Peyton Winn continued her standout season as Portsmouth captured a 25-22, 26-24, 25-19 victory. Winn finished with four aces, 10 kills and four blocks and Kamryn Lehner steered the offense with two aces, five digs and 20 assists. Audrey Abedon added three aces, seven kills and 14 digs.

Portsmouth and East Providence are back in action on Wednesday at South Kingstown and Classical.

The Crusaders were led by Brooke Rutherford, who dished out 18 assists, while Gabby Andrade anchored the defense with 22 digs. Josie Torok added six kills to help power the offense to the straight-sets win (25-22, 25-20, 25-20).

The Avengers were paced by Sarah Nula and Sasha Lattenist, who each recorded three kills and three digs.

The play of Olivia Majeau (20 assists, 6 aces and 4 kills) and Quin Crowshaw (5 aces and 5 kills) helped secure the Northmen's sweep (25-9, 25-13 and 25-19) of the Broncos

title: Jalen Williams reveals he's fully cleared from lingering hamstring problems
description: Jalen Williams reveals he's fully cleared from lingering hamstring problems.
fullText:
Hoping for a clean slate, Jalen Williams sang music to fans' ears. The Oklahoma City Thunder held their 2026-27 Media Day. One of the bigger storylines of the all-day event? The All-NBA talent's health. After an injury-plagued year, he hopes the summer off has him ready to get back on track.

The Thunder fell five wins shy of their back-to-back ambitions last year. Williams' health is viewed as the biggest reason why that was the case. Two wrist surgeries and four hamstring strains limited him to 33 regular-season games and five NBA playoff games.

"That was one of the big things. I had never really had any injuries that set me back. Looking back on my hamstring injury, for people who don't know, it's a touch-and-go thing," Williams said. "It's not like I'm pulling my hamstring in December where I can take all this time. It's like I'm pulling my hamstring sometimes in the middle of the playoffs."

Williams revealed that his latest hamstring strain — the fourth in a five-month span — is completely healed. He estimated that it happened sometime around mid-June. Which means, yes, he likely would've returned in a hypothetical 2026 NBA Finals matchup against the New York Knicks. But I digress.

Once Williams moved past the disappointment of his body betraying him, he went into the lab. Alongside the Thunder and their best medical staff members, they dove into the science and figured out a plan to make sure last year was a one-time anomaly and not the start of a disturbing trend with his lower body. He even held workouts with Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's personal NBA trainer to ensure he exhausted every option to avoid another nightmare season.

"It's more just about rest and understanding my body and some of the cues to let me know that my hamstrings are going to get tight or understanding that it's not just my hamstring," Williams said. "Trying to open up my hips a little more and do stuff that I've been doing throughout my whole year. Just understanding my body more and more every year. So that if I have signs during the year, I can address them right away and know what to do."

That's interesting to hear. Love it when NBA players dive into the minutiae of their actual routine. Williams provided a little peek behind the curtain of what last year's injury woes were like. The Thunder did an incredible job of overcoming his absence for most of the year. But it eventually came back to bite them at the biggest stage. Not having an All-Star-level go-to scorer eventually booted them from the NBA playoffs.

"I don't look at anything as a setback. For me, it sucks more so that I work really hard at what I do. For me to not even be able to play just because of injury kinda sucks," Williams said. "But at the same time, what's meant for you will come back. All I can do is control my attitude, my effort going into it and what I do to respond to it. That's kinda it."

title: Protect College Sports Act passes U.S. Senate vote, House next up
description: The Protect College Sports Act aims to create some concise solutions to the wild world of college football and other collegiate sports. The U.S. legislative measure is now one step closer to becoming a reality. On Monday night, the U.
fullText:
The Protect College Sports Act aims to create some concise solutions to the wild world of college football and other collegiate sports. The U.S. legislative measure is now one step closer to becoming a reality.

On Monday night, the U.S. Senate pushed forward the PCSA with a 77-22 vote. However, voting in the House of Representatives still needs to take place in order to clear both chambers of Congress.

The PCSA has become a talking point in college sports over recent months with NIL and transfer portal chaos creating significant issues in football, college basketball and other sports. President Donald Trump has been making his rounds at sporting events, including Texas' win over Tennessee at Neyland Stadium this past weekend.

Trump's been a major proponent for the bill, and Texas senator Ted Cruz recently suggested that the U.S. president will sign the bill live on ESPN's College GameDay if it passes the Senate and House.

MORE: Senators propose coach salary cap for Protect College Sports Act

United States President Donald Trump is shown on the video board at Neyland Stadium before the game. Mandatory Credit: Randy Sartin-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)

Top conferences like the Big Ten and SEC have heavily pushed for the act to move forward with NIL's uncertainty. Many programs are having issues navigating the new world of college sports with players leaving schools yearly.

Cruz and Washington senator Maria Cantwell co-wrote the bipartisan bill, which is a step closer to hitting the House floor. Meanwhile, CBS Sports indicates that could be months away with the House of Representatives reportedly not scheduled to return until November 9.

"This bill puts an end to the chaos plaguing college athletics," Cruz said Monday. "It protects NIL opportunities because student-athletes deserve the opportunity to benefit from their talent without being taken advantage of by unscrupulous agents and backdoor deals … It prevents the most powerful and wealthy conferences from breaking away to form a super league. But most importantly, it protects our student-athletes."

The biggest aspects of the bill that are being pushed include transfer and eligibility rules, as well as NIL regulations. Meanwhile, NCAA antitrust protection is another sticking point as the governing body looks to restore order with athlete compensation.

MORE: Ted Cruz plans for Donald Trump to sign Protect College Sports Act on ESPN show

The clock is still ticking on the PCSA, though, considering a new Congress is sworn in January 3. It's not impossible for Congress to get a deal done prior to that date, but time is certainly running quickly.

title: O'Neill 'positive' as NI maintain unbeaten start
description: Michael O'Neill says he is "positive" as Northern Ireland maintain their unbeaten start in the Nations League with a goalless draw with Hungary.
fullText:
After 315 days away from Windsor Park, Northern Ireland's goalless draw with Hungary on their homecoming did not have the same drama as the late win over Georgia on Friday night.

But that suited Northern Ireland just fine.

On their return to League B in the Nations League, they sit joint-top with Ukraine with four points from their opening two matches.

It's a result that left manager Michael O'Neill feeling "positive" at the halfway point of the four-game window.

"We played a very good side, I thought we were more than a match for the opposition," said O'Neill on Hungary, who lost their opener 1-0 to Ukraine on Friday.

"It's another clean sheet for us, which is positive, but we just couldn't find maybe enough to create that clear-cut chance that we'd win the game."

Northern Ireland top group despite Hungary stalemate

Chances were at a premium at Windsor Park as both defences came out on top.

Patrick Kelly hit the crossbar in the first half for Northern Ireland, and Isaac Price had an effort beaten away by Balazs Toth.

After Dan Ballard controversially conceded a penalty in Georgia, Shea Charles also had a penalty appeal waved away in the lead-up to the Kelly chance for a similar incident.

While O'Neill said he had yet to see it back, he did quip that "the referee never seems to make the walk for us to the side of the pitch. It never seems to happen for us."

The threat of Liverpool midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai was largely nullified throughout the game as Hungary, like Northern Ireland, struggled to create any clear-cut chances.

The only save that Pierce Charles had to make in goal was when a lethargic clearance led to Alex Toth shooting towards goal in the closing stages, but the QPR stopper was otherwise untroubled.

After a 5,000-mile trip from Georgia in their opening game, Northern Ireland had to quickly reset and O'Neill admitted he saw "two tired teams" at the end of the game.

"I think our preparation, our first game in terms of being away from home and everything, was more difficult.

"I felt like Hungary got a little bit stronger towards the end."

One point that did irk O'Neill was perceived play acting from some of the visiting players.

Ethan Galbraith, captain Shea Charles, Jamie Donley and Isaac Price were all booked by Spanish referee Ricardo de Burgos, and O'Neill felt the visitors played their part in a stop-start game.

"I was disappointed with some of the yellow cards that were given, and I was disappointed with some of the Hungarian players' behaviour on the pitch, holding their face and screaming," O'Neill said.

"Really, there was no need for that. It was an honest, competitive game. We didn't need the nature of the simulation or the antics.

"We want that away and out of the game. That's why the referee has to speed the game up."

Northern Ireland are back on the road in their third game of the quadruple-header when they face Ukraine in Slovakia on Friday.

It will be another difficult test for a youthful Northern Ireland side, but for now O'Neill is pleased with what he described as a "great start".

"It's a very good start in a very, very competitive group," he added.

"If you look at the results so far, you can see that. The teams seem very well matched."

title: Infantino makes bigger cash pledge to Fifa members
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino indicates more money could be distributed to the governing body's members from its cash reserves.
fullText:
Gianni Infantino has indicated a greater amount of money could be distributed to Fifa members from its estimated £4.4bn cash reserves.

In a letter seen by BBC Sport, and sent to the governing body's six continental confederations on Monday, Fifa president Infantino said he would support "the greatest level of additional funding that can responsibly be delivered".

Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan, which proposed selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, sparking a major backlash.

His letter comes after Uefa and Concacaf - the confederations for Europe and North America, Central America and the Caribbean - demanded Fifa pays $10m (£7.5m) to all 211 members from its reserves.

The proposal will be considered by the Fifa Council when they meet on 15 October.

"I will not prejudge the amount," Infantino said in the letter.

"A single figure can begin the discussion, but it cannot complete a global policy."

Infantino issued his latest defence of the failed proposal to sell a slice of the World Cup commercial rights that brought calls for his resignation, again claiming it had been intended to generate additional money for the game.

"The recent commercial proposal, now withdrawn, was intended to enable Fifa to invest 

Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan, and called for an independent review of FFE.

Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate.

fullText:
GPT-6.1 Astra showed deceptive behavior and tried to use external tools despite knowing it would be unsafe

OpenAI is scrapping the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation ⁠AI model planned for an October debut, over safety concerns raised by researchers ⁠during internal testing, the ⁠Wall ​Street Journal reported on Monday.

The model, expected to appear in ChatGPT and ⁠Codex, was designed to handle more complex tasks without human assistance, the report said.

Earlier this ⁠month, Dario Amodei, the Anthropic CEO, called for the industry ​to slow the development ‌of frontier ‌AI models to allow safety measures to keep pace, a ‌view endorsed by Sam Altman, the OpenAI CEO, and Elon Musk, the SpaceX CEO.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

Saachi Jain, the ChatGPT parent’s safety chief, told the Journal on Monday ‌that Astra fell short of the company’s standards in alignment tests, which assess whether a ​system follows human intent.

The model showed more deception than its predecessor, including at times failing to accurately disclose actions it had or had not taken, the report ⁠said.

It also had problems with “scope authorization”, pushing ahead with ​tasks ​without requesting user permission ​and sometimes attempting to use external tools ​or services ‌when doing so could ​be ​unsafe.

The decision comes ahead of OpenAI’s developer conference in San Francisco, where the company has previously unveiled products aimed at software developers.

title: Meta’s AI agent Muse gives out user’s home address without permission, sending buyer to his house
description:
The new AI agent, Muse, was released last week and has been downloaded by 3 million users
When Usman asked if a keyboard for sale on Facebook Marketplace was still available on Saturday, he received an enthusiastic and immediate response.
“Yep still available!” wrote Matt Robb.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
The new AI agent, Muse, was released last week and has been downloaded by 3 million users

When Usman asked if a keyboard for sale on Facebook Marketplace was still available on Saturday, he received an enthusiastic and immediate response.

“Yep still available!” wrote Matt Robb.

The two agreed on a price, and Robb sent his Toronto address. Usman, wife and daughter in tow, showed up several hours later at Robb’s home and sent a text that he had arrived.

Robb responded, “yep I’m here!”, but he was not at home. Nobody walked out of the apartment building.

Usman sent Robb a picture of the building’s door and wrote, “Hello???? I am standing outside.” After 20 minutes of no face-to-face contact, he abandoned the sale. “Man if you didn’t want to sell it why did you waste my time man,” he wrote, and drove away.

An hour later, Robb, or who Usman thought was Robb, responded apologetically. “Hey really sorry about tonight, got tied up and missed you completely,” read the message, which the Guardian reviewed.

Usman had not contacted the real Robb. Throughout the daylong interaction, the human version of Robb never knew Usman had messaged him or had agreed to buy the keyboard. He did not know Usman had received his address or that he was waiting outside his apartment building.

Usman had spoken to Meta’s new AI agent, Muse, released 22 September in the US and downloaded 3m times. The company advertises the semi-autonomous AI product as a personal assistant.

Without Robb’s consent or approval, Muse had given out his home address, creating the false impression that Robb was expecting the would-be buyer at his apartment, he said.

The first message Robb actually sent Usman came 24 hours later, once he realized what had happened.

“Hey man I’m really sorry for the other day,” the message, which the Guardian reviewed, said. “I activated muse metas new Al and it literally took control of my Facebook marketplace and it gave you my address. Genuinely didn’t even know it had arranged for you to come to my literal apartment it didn’t ask me for approval.”

Robb, a consumer tech reviewer, had seen Meta advertise Muse’s ability to automate his Marketplace listings and decided to take advantage of it. He input his address as the pickup location but said he never gave Muse permission to share it with potential buyers. Muse was also negotiating on his behalf without seeking approval, accepting lowball offers, he said.

Robb said he never received any heads-up from the agent about the transaction or the meetup. He never knew that Usman was en route to his house.

Usman told the Guardian he thought he was speaking to Robb the whole time.

Robb shared screenshots of Muse’s interaction with Usman on Threads, the text-based social network owned by Meta. David Singleton, the co-founder and CEO of Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, tweeted that he has been in touch with Robb. Singleton said that, when investigating similar reports, the company has “consistently learned that Muse was following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission. Would love to help and figure out what’s going on here!” Robb confirmed Singleton reached out but hasn’t heard back since he initially responded to him.

Muse ultimately admitted to Robb that he never gave it permission to share his address. “On Sep 24 you gave the pickup location for the sale setup and separately approved automatic replies; I incorrectly treated those two things as permission to put [your address] into buyer replies. I never asked for consent.”

Robb said he assumed that, because Meta owned Marketplace, Muse and Messenger, there would be an integration that would make it clear when other users were speaking to an AI agent or that messages would be clearly marked as being sent by Muse. Meta AI, another of the company’s AI products, makes it obvious a user is conversing with a chatbot.

“But Muse is doing something else,” he said. “It’s almost imitating me.”

After the incident with Usman, Robb told Muse to stop giving his address. To test the bot, he asked a few friends to see if Muse would still share it. 

 “And it literally gave my address out to five people,” he said.

In addition to sharing his address and inviting a stranger to his home without his approval, Muse also made up information. The AI agent, responding as Robb, told Usman that Robb was home when he was not, then apologized with a fabrication about being too busy.

“The worst part was Muse actually replied: ‘I’m right here, like waiting for you,’” Robb said. “It made it so much worse because I don’t know if the guy thought I was messing with him.”

While a great deal of attention has been paid to the ways frontier AI models are going rogue, Meta’s agent is an AI product in the hands of millions of everyday consumers, many of whom have given it their private information.

title: ‘New kind of cyber incident’: OpenAI apologises for Medicare hack and reveals extent of agents’ attack
description: Chief strategy officer to fly to Australia to front joint committee on AI after breaches of government...
fullText:
Chief strategy officer to fly to Australia to front joint committee on AI after breaches of government websites

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

OpenAI has apologised to Australians for its agent attack on Medicare, and will front parliament next week, as the tech company revealed more details about its June hack of Australian government websites.

In a blog post released on Tuesday, OpenAI said it should have handled its response better.

“We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future.”

The company also provided more detail on the incident revealed by the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, last week.

OpenAI said it became aware of agent activity on Australian government websites in mid-August after the company reviewed earlier training incidents after the Hugging Face attack in July.

The agents gained non-public access to a Services Australia portal for Medicare statistics, and OpenAI said the agent was able to run commands, retrieve internal files, credentials, and write files, but no patient or client records were accessed.

The NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research’s public crime mapping tool was also accessed, with application configuration, operational jobs and logs and website metadata provided to the agency.

The agent discovered an exposed access key to query the Victorian agency for health information’s reporting system to access aggregate survey statistics.

For the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, OpenAI agents retrieved aggregate statistics, but separate attempts to bypass access controls were unsuccessful and the information obtained was publicly available.

Services Australia and the Victorian health department were informed on 10 September, while the NSW bureau of crime stastistics was informed on 18 September.

The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare was not informed until 24 September, as OpenAI deemed it did not meet disclosure thresholds.

“Since then we’ve worked closely with Australian government agencies to share what we’ve learned to date,” OpenAI said. “If we identify any additional affected agencies, we will notify them promptly and directly with the information available and provide updates as further facts emerge.”

The incident occurred after one model was tasked to research government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victoria. The model had difficulty obtaining that information, and OpenAI said “it took actions that we had not authorised it to take” including accessing Services Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service.

OpenAI said it would commit resources and expertise to affected agencies, and provide Australian government agencies with support to build cyberdefences on critical infrastructure.

Australian government agencies and industries will also be given credits out of OpenAI’s US$1bn (AU$1.4bn) Daybreak fund, which lets those organisations use frontier AI for cyberdefence, and to harden their systems by reviewing code and system configurations for potential vulnerabilities that can then be patched.

The company said it would also establish a taskforce with Australian expertise to develop practical policy recommendations on managing risk with AI agents.

OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will appear at the Joint Select Committee on AI on Tuesday next week. Guardian Australia reported on Monday that Anthropic would also appear at this hearing, but not at a Senate inquiry into AI and datacentres this week.

Albanese who was in the United States last week when he announced the hack, said at the time he had spoken with OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, “to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident”.

On Tuesday, Albanese said OpenAI had been “very constructive and open in engaging” since the incident, as had Anthropic. He said AI can improve economic growth and productivity but it also carries risks.

“And we’ve seen those risks exposed – not just in what occurred in Australia, but the revelation that has occurred in the United States and other countries as well.”

The federal government has flagged it could introduce mandatory reporting rules for AI-related data breaches, after the revelation OpenAI used a public-facing email address three months after the hack to report the incident to Services Australia.

The company said on Tuesday it had “a lot of work ahead” to rebuild trust with Australians but said it was making “meaningful changes”.
